title: Large-Scale ChatBot Validation Through Customer Digital Twin Simulations
summary: LLM-based chatbots are transforming customer service in regulated domains such as banking, but scalable and cost-effective validation remains a critical barrier to safe deployment. We present a two-part contribution for large-scale chatbot validation. First, we introduce a methodology for creating high-fidelity synthetic customer agents (SCAs) as digital twins, grounded in real transactional and conversational data, that enables automatic generation and behavioral conditioning to simulate diverse customer profiles and interaction styles. Evaluation demonstrates that SCAs achieve high semantic alignment with real customers, low hallucination rates, and successful personality trait reproduction with controllable interventions. Second, we develop an SCA-based validation framework combining automated LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, human expert testing, and adversarial probing. Scenario-based validation across emotional states, demographic groups, and linguistic factors confirms robust performance. Our approach was used to validate a customer facing chatbot at a leading UK bank, providing financial institutions with a scalable pathway toward regulatory compliance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable way to validate bank customer-service LLM chatbots using synthetic customer agents built from real data plus an automated testing framework.
AI.motivation: LLM chatbots are being deployed in tightly regulated sectors like banking, where mistakes are costly and regulators demand evidence of safety and fairness. Manual validation is expensive and does not scale to the vast space of customer types, emotions, and scenarios. The authors aim to create a scalable, systematic validation process that satisfies regulatory and safety requirements while remaining cost‑effective.
AI.method: The authors build Synthetic Customer Agents (SCAs) as digital twins of real customers, using real transactional and conversational data to ground them. SCAs are designed to support automatic dialogue generation, behavioral conditioning, and personality control, so they can mimic diverse customer profiles and interaction styles. They then embed these SCAs into a validation framework that mixes LLM-as-a-Judge scoring, human expert review, and adversarial probing. The system runs scenario-based tests across emotional states, demographics, and linguistic variations to assess the chatbot’s performance and robustness.
AI.result: The SCAs show high semantic similarity to real customers, low hallucination/error rates, and reproduce personality traits with controllable interventions. The combined framework yields robust validation across varied scenarios and user types, and was successfully applied to validate a production banking chatbot at a major UK bank.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic, data-grounded customer agents can effectively stand in for real users when validating LLM chatbots, enabling scalable, systematic, and relatively low-cost testing. Coupled with automated judging, expert review, and adversarial stress tests, this provides a practical path for financial institutions to demonstrate safety and regulatory compliance of customer-facing LLM systems.

title: Do Methods Support the Claims? Intra-Paper Verification for Peer Review
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Source code, prompts, evaluation materials, and supporting data available at https://github.com/Ranjitha2493/intra-paper-claim-method-verification
summary: The growing volume of scientific submissions has motivated interest in using large language models (LLMs) to assist peer review. Existing automated novelty assessment approaches typically compare a paper's claimed contributions against prior literature, implicitly assuming that these contributions are accurately realized in the work itself. Human reviewers, however, frequently challenge novelty claims not because similar ideas already exist, but because the methodological evidence presented in the paper does not adequately support them. This internal mismatch between claimed contributions and methodological realization is rarely examined by current LLM-based review systems. To address this gap, we introduce intra-paper claim verification, a framework that evaluates whether novelty claims articulated in a paper are substantiated by the methods used to realize them. The framework employs an LLM to extract novelty claims from the introduction, retrieve claim-relevant methodological evidence, and assess whether the methods substantiate the stated contributions. Assessment is guided by reviewer-inspired evaluation criteria derived inductively from human peer reviews collected from 182 ICLR 2025 papers. These criteria capture recurring reviewer concerns related to novelty, methodology, clarity, and other issues and are used to generate structured reviewer-style assessments of claim substantiation. We evaluate the framework by comparing LLM-generated review comments against human reviewer concerns on a balanced subset of accepted and rejected papers. Human evaluation demonstrates significant alignment between framework-generated assessments and human reviewer concerns, particularly for novelty-related issues. BERTScore further distinguishes corresponding human-LLM review pairs from mismatched controls, indicating that the framework captures concerns consistent with human reviewer observations.

AI.tldr: They propose an LLM-based framework that checks whether a paper’s novelty claims are actually supported by its own methods, and show its outputs align well with real reviewers’ concerns.
AI.motivation: Current LLM tools for peer review focus mainly on comparing a paper’s claimed contributions to prior work to judge novelty. They largely assume that the paper’s methods correctly implement and support those claims. However, human reviewers often reject or criticize papers not because the idea exists elsewhere, but because the methodology, experiments, or analysis do not really substantiate the claimed contributions. This internal claim–evidence mismatch within a single paper is underexplored by existing automated systems. The authors aim to fill this gap so that automated peer-review assistance better mirrors human reviewer reasoning about whether claims are backed by appropriate methods.
AI.method: They define an “intra-paper claim verification” framework. First, an LLM automatically extracts novelty claims from the introduction of a paper. Then it retrieves the parts of the methods section that are relevant to each claim. Using reviewer-inspired criteria—inductively derived from human reviews of 182 ICLR 2025 submissions and covering novelty, methodology, clarity, and related dimensions—the LLM judges whether the methodological evidence actually supports each claim. The system outputs structured, reviewer-like assessments focused on claim substantiation. They then evaluate this framework by comparing the LLM’s generated comments with actual human reviewer concerns on a curated, balanced set of accepted and rejected papers, and analyze alignment quantitatively (BERTScore) and via human assessment.
AI.result: Human evaluators found that the assessments produced by the framework align strongly with real reviewer concerns, especially those pertaining to novelty. Quantitatively, BERTScore can reliably distinguish matched human–LLM review pairs from mismatched ones, implying that the model’s comments are closer in content to the actual reviewers’ notes on the same paper than to notes on different papers. This suggests that the framework is able to capture and reproduce concern patterns similar to those raised by human reviewers.
AI.conclusion: Intra-paper claim verification—checking whether a paper’s own methods substantiate its novelty claims—can be effectively automated with LLMs. By leveraging reviewer-derived criteria and structured evaluation of claim–method alignment, the framework produces review-style feedback that meaningfully parallels human reviewer concerns, particularly around novelty. This indicates its potential as a useful assistive tool in peer review workflows, complementing traditional literature-based novelty checks by focusing on internal consistency and evidential support within a single paper.

title: DuplexGen: Adaptive Synthesis of Human-AI Turn-Taking Dialogues
summary: Turn-taking is a central component of full-duplex interaction. Which turn-taking behaviors are appropriate varies with the scenario, yet current models apply a single norm regardless of context. This limitation originates in their training data: human-human speech corpora capture natural timing phenomena but provide little role grounding or scenario-specific norms, while heuristic or prompted synthesis methods inject turn-taking behaviors without basing them on human preferences. We introduce DuplexGen, a framework for generating dialogues with scenario-adaptive turn-taking by calibrating LLM predictions against a small set of slot-level human preference annotations. In six cooperative and competitive tasks, human turn-taking preferences differ systematically, and DuplexGen aligns substantially more closely with those preferences than uncalibrated prompting or training solely on generic human-human data; a full-duplex model trained on DuplexGen-generated data exhibits distinctive, human-preferred turn-taking behaviors. These results show that human calibration, not corpus scale or prompt design alone, is what allows turn-taking synthesis to be scenario-specific.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DuplexGen, a framework that generates scenario-adaptive turn-taking behavior for full-duplex dialogue systems by calibrating LLM outputs with a small amount of human preference data, outperforming generic corpora and uncalibrated prompting.
AI.motivation: Existing full-duplex dialogue models use a single, context-agnostic turn-taking norm because they are trained either on human-human corpora (which lack clear role and scenario grounding) or on synthetic data driven by heuristics/prompts that are not validated against human preferences. However, appropriate turn-taking behavior varies systematically across scenarios (e.g., cooperative vs. competitive tasks), so models need a way to adapt their timing and interruption patterns to the interaction context while being grounded in what humans actually prefer.
AI.method:
They propose DuplexGen, a data-generation framework that:
1) Defines specific interaction scenarios and roles (e.g., cooperative vs. competitive tasks).
2) Uses a large language model to generate dialogues with varied turn-taking behaviors in those scenarios.
3) Collects a small set of human annotations at the slot/segment level indicating preferred turn-taking patterns.
4) Calibrates or conditions the LLM’s dialogue generation using these human preference signals so the synthesized dialogues reflect scenario-specific turn-taking norms.
They then train a full-duplex dialogue model on this DuplexGen-generated, human-calibrated data and evaluate it against baselines using uncalibrated prompting or generic human-human corpora.
AI.result: Across six cooperative and competitive tasks, they find systematic differences in human preferences for turn-taking behaviors depending on the scenario. DuplexGen-generated data, calibrated with small-scale human annotations, leads to dialogue systems whose turn-taking aligns much more closely with these measured human preferences than systems trained on generic human-human corpora or using uncalibrated LLM prompting. A full-duplex model trained on DuplexGen data exhibits distinctive, scenario-appropriate, and human-preferred timing behaviors (e.g., how and when to take or yield the floor).
AI.conclusion: Scenario-specific turn-taking in full-duplex systems cannot be achieved reliably through corpus scale or clever prompt design alone. Instead, explicitly calibrating LLM-based data generation with targeted human preference annotations is key. DuplexGen demonstrates that a modest amount of human feedback at the slot level is sufficient to synthesize training data that yields full-duplex models with adaptive, human-preferred turn-taking behavior across diverse interaction scenarios.

title: Choosing Where and How to Moderate: End-to-End Trade-offs in Filter Placement and Response Rewriting
summary: Content-moderation classifiers are usually evaluated in isolation, but deployment requires choosing where to intervene and what follows a flag. We evaluate these choices using two end-to-end customer-outcome metrics rather than component accuracy: Usefulness, the fraction of turns with a shown, non-harmful, relevant response, and Harmful Exposure, the fraction with a shown harmful response. Latency and error rates are diagnostics. We compare Input only, Response only, and Input + response hard blocking on a human-labelled product benchmark and public ToxicChat evaluation. At the evaluated operating points, Response only achieves the highest filter-only Usefulness in both settings, while Input + response achieves lower Harmful Exposure. Replacing Response only blocking with Response + rewrite recovers most blocked traffic and yields the same observed Harmful Exposure count as Response only blocking for the selected configuration; this equality is not an equivalence result. Probe routing substantially reduces conditional route-and-generation time relative to LLM routing at comparable measured outcomes. A focused output review shows how rewrites balance filter passage with usefulness by generalizing triggering language while retaining benign intent and safe redirection; some sensitive-domain outputs nevertheless omit potentially safety-relevant support information. These results support comparing moderation configurations under deployment-specific safety and latency constraints rather than applying a universal placement rule. Code and public artifacts are available at https://github.com/microsoft/mod-frontier

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates different content moderation configurations end-to-end, focusing on user outcomes instead of just classifier accuracy, and finds that response-based blocking and rewriting can optimize usefulness while controlling harmful exposure under deployment-specific constraints.
AI.motivation: Traditional evaluations of content moderation models focus on classifier accuracy in isolation, ignoring how and where moderation is deployed in a real system and what happens after content is flagged. The authors aim to fill this gap by proposing user-centric, end-to-end metrics and systematically comparing practical moderation configurations under realistic constraints.
AI.method: The authors define two primary customer-outcome metrics: Usefulness (fraction of turns with a shown, non-harmful, relevant response) and Harmful Exposure (fraction of turns with a shown harmful response). They benchmark several moderation strategies—Input-only blocking, Response-only blocking, and combined Input + Response blocking—on a human-labeled product dataset and the public ToxicChat benchmark. They also experiment with replacing simple blocking with response rewriting, and compare probe-based routing against LLM-based routing for efficiency, along with a focused qualitative review of model rewrites.
AI.result: Response-only blocking achieves the highest usefulness among filter-only strategies in both the internal and ToxicChat evaluations, while combining input and response blocking yields the lowest harmful exposure. Switching from pure response blocking to response blocking plus rewriting recovers most of the otherwise blocked traffic while keeping the measured harmful exposure count equal for the evaluated configuration. Probe routing notably reduces routing and generation latency at comparable measured safety and usefulness outcomes. Qualitative analysis shows that rewrites typically preserve benign intent and provide safe redirection, but sometimes omit potentially important safety-support information in sensitive domains.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end, user-outcome–focused evaluation is essential for choosing content moderation configurations; no single universal rule for where to place moderation filters is optimal for all deployments. Response-focused strategies, especially when augmented with rewriting and efficient probe routing, can provide strong trade-offs between usefulness, harmful exposure, and latency, but designers must tune configurations to domain-specific safety needs and carefully review behavior in sensitive areas.

title: Probing the Origins of Reasoning Performance: Representational Quality for Mathematical Problem-Solving in RL vs. SFT Fine-Tuned Models
summary: Large reasoning models trained via reinforcement learning (RL) have been increasingly shown to outperform their supervised fine-tuned (SFT) counterparts on mathematical reasoning tasks; Yet the mechanistic basis for this advantage remains unclear. We therefore ask, what internal representational differences enable RL models' superior performance? Our work presents two converging lines of evidence: First, linear probes trained on layer-wise hidden states reveal that RL models tend to achieve higher accuracy in predicting answer correctness compared to SFT models, indicating more linearly separable and structured representations. Second, mean ablation studies show that RL models develop a hierarchical architecture where deeper layers become progressively more critical, whereas SFT models distribute importance uniformly across layers. Together, these findings demonstrate that RL training fundamentally restructures how models represent and process reasoning problems. Finally, we analyze token-count variability under repeated sampling across problems to assess adaptive compute allocation. While we observe higher variability in some RL-tuned models than in their SFT counterparts, we see strong consistency in others, suggesting that token allocation may depend more on the overall training pipeline than on RL versus SFT alone. We believe this token-allocation variability reveals the spread of plausible on-policy reasoning, highlighting which models exhibit stable policies versus those that are under-determined, potentially non-identifiable solution behaviour.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why reinforcement learning–tuned large reasoning models outperform supervised fine-tuned models on math reasoning, showing RL leads to more linearly separable internal representations, a deeper-layer–centric hierarchy of importance, and distinct token allocation behavior during inference.
AI.motivation: Although RL-trained reasoning models often surpass supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models on mathematical tasks, it is unclear what internal representation changes account for this performance gap. The authors aim to open the black box by identifying structural and mechanistic differences in how RL and SFT models internally encode correctness and allocate computation, rather than only reporting external benchmark scores.
AI.method: They compare RL and SFT models using: (1) linear probes trained on hidden states at each layer to predict whether an answer is correct, assessing the linear separability and structure of representations; (2) mean ablation experiments that systematically suppress layer activations to measure how performance degrades, revealing how importance is distributed across depth; and (3) an analysis of token-count variability under repeated sampling for the same problems to infer how adaptively each model allocates computation (longer or shorter chains of thought) and how stable their on-policy reasoning is.
AI.result: Linear probes show RL models achieve higher accuracy in predicting answer correctness from hidden states, indicating more structured and linearly separable internal representations than SFT models. Mean ablation reveals that RL models acquire a hierarchical architecture in which deeper layers are progressively more critical, whereas SFT models spread importance relatively uniformly across layers. Token-count variability analyses find that some RL models exhibit higher variability than SFT counterparts, but others are similarly stable, suggesting that adaptive token allocation is influenced by the broader training pipeline rather than RL vs SFT alone.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning fundamentally changes how large reasoning models internally represent and process reasoning problems: it sharpens correctness-related features into more linearly separable representations and concentrates critical computation in deeper layers, forming a clear hierarchy of importance. However, RL is not solely responsible for adaptive compute allocation patterns, as token-count variability depends strongly on training details beyond the RL/SFT distinction. Token variability can be interpreted as reflecting the diversity and stability of on-policy reasoning strategies, distinguishing models with stable policies from those with under-determined or non-identifiable solution behaviors.

title: Characterizing Human-Likeness in AI Generated Poetry: A Zero-shot Classification Study
summary: With the advancement of AI technologies, Generative AI (GenAI) and human written text have become nearly indistinguishable. Additionally, the global standardization of AI chatbots made academic malpractice more frequent. Furthermore, existing research indicates GenAI poems are the most difficult to distinguish even without any modification thus, GenAI poems are naturally deemed human-like by modern detectors. However, the objectivity of such dissertations needs to be verified against modern detection tools but the subjectivity of poetry and the black-box nature of the modern LLMs (Large Language Models) architectures made verification of such work quite complicated. Hence, the main objective of the research is to deduce the attributes of English poetry that contribute classification and misclassification of both human and AI poems and provide corroborating or contradicting evidence to the poetry distinguishability claim. For such characterizations, we propose a Zero-shot detection pipeline with a dataset consisting of both human and AI poems to verify the distinguishability of human and AI creation and extract the aforementioned crucial attributes for accurate classification. Extraction of such attributes provides benefits in two ways: firstly, it reduces the margin of training needed as only the poems based on misclassifying attributes need to be trained and fine tuned and finally provides a critical insight to the GenAI detection dilemma to strengthen the modern detection pipelines.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to distinguish AI-generated English poems from human-written ones and identifies poem attributes that cause correct or incorrect classification.
AI.motivation: As GenAI and human text become nearly indistinguishable—especially poetry—academic malpractice risk increases, while prior claims that GenAI poems are hard to detect lack verification with modern tools. The authors want to objectively test these claims and understand what linguistic or stylistic features lead detectors to classify or misclassify poems as human or AI.
AI.method: They build a zero-shot detection pipeline that uses contemporary detection models on a curated dataset of English poems containing both human-written and AI-generated examples. They then analyze the detector outputs to extract and characterize poem attributes that are associated with correct classifications and with misclassifications.
AI.result: The pipeline can empirically measure how distinguishable human and AI poems are and identify specific poem features that systematically lead to accurate detection or to confusion (misclassification) by current systems.
AI.conclusion: By revealing which attributes matter most for classifying poems, the study both narrows the amount of training data needed—focusing on poems with problematic attributes—and offers actionable insights to improve and strengthen modern GenAI detection pipelines for poetic text.

title: Even More Deception: Objective Misalignment in Mixed-Motive LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs)-powered multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed in mixed-motive environments, where agents operate under asymmetric information and strategic deception due to conflicting or hidden objectives. In these settings, misalignment with collective goals becomes a central concern. We propose a novel framework for evaluating objective misalignment using the social deduction game Werewolf, modifying the objective of a single agent while preserving its assigned role. Across LLMs from four different model families and sizes, four player roles, and three objective formulations, we introduce a dual analysis of the agents' internal reasoning and their public cheap-talk behavior (i.e costless, non-binding communication that does not directly affect the agents' utilities), complemented by an analysis of game outcomes. Our results show that objective misalignment undermines outcomes in inherently adversarial environments, an effect exacerbated by asymmetric information and specialized roles. While compromised agents consistently develop distinct objective-dependent reasoning strategies, these adaptations remain largely invisible in their public behavior. More broadly, our findings suggest that even subtle objective misalignment can profoundly affect collective decision-making, highlighting the need for effective mitigation strategies for LLM-based multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the social deduction game Werewolf to study how changing one LLM agent’s objective (while keeping its role fixed) affects behavior and group outcomes in multi-agent systems with hidden information and strategic deception.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly used in environments where agents may have hidden or conflicting goals, creating risks that individual objectives become misaligned with the collective goal. Existing evaluations often focus on single-agent benchmarks or do not directly probe the consequences of subtle objective misalignment under asymmetric information and deception. The authors want a controlled, game-based testbed to understand how such misalignment manifests in reasoning, communication, and overall system performance.
AI.method: They construct a multi-agent evaluation framework based on the social deduction game Werewolf. One agent’s objective is modified (misaligned) while keeping its in-game role unchanged. They test various LLM families and sizes, four different player roles, and three ways of formulating objectives. The analysis is dual: (1) they inspect internal reasoning traces produced by the models; (2) they analyze public cheap-talk communication among agents, and they also study resulting game outcomes. This allows them to compare what agents ‘think’ internally vs. what they say publicly when one of them has a misaligned objective.
AI.result: Objective misalignment significantly degrades outcomes in this inherently adversarial game, particularly under conditions of asymmetric information and role specialization. Misaligned (compromised) agents systematically develop reasoning strategies that differ from aligned agents and depend on their altered objective. However, these strategic differences in internal reasoning are not clearly reflected in their observable public cheap-talk messages, which remain mostly indistinguishable from aligned behavior.
AI.conclusion: Even small or subtle changes in an agent’s objective can have large negative effects on collective decision-making in LLM-based multi-agent systems, especially in settings with hidden information and adversarial incentives. Because misalignment shows up clearly in internal reasoning but not in public communication, it may be hard to detect via surface behavior alone. Therefore, robust mitigation and monitoring strategies are needed when deploying LLM multi-agent systems in mixed-motive environments.

title: Steering Instruction Hierarchies at Inference Time
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM '26; the first two authors contributed equally to the work. 24 pages, 9 figures
summary: Instruction hierarchies are a core safety assumption of language model deployment: higher priority inputs, such as system prompts, should override conflicting lower priority inputs from users or tools. Yet frontier LLMs often violate this hierarchy. We introduce V-Steer, a training-free inference time method that restores privileged influence by editing cached value vectors at prompt positions. Using direct logit attribution on the first next token prediction, V-Steer identifies heads where lower priority spans dominate privileged ones, then boosts privileged spans and suppresses conflicting lower priority spans through in-place multiplicative edits to cached V tensors. Since the method acts only on cached values, it remains compatible with fused attention backends and adds only a one time prefill overhead. Across models from 7B to 70B, this attribution guided intervention raises primary constraint accuracy from under 18% up to 92% on controlled role conflict benchmarks, and on broader instruction hierarchy evaluations substantially outperforms prompt only baselines while matching or exceeding SoTA training based methods on 3 of 4 scales of LLMs, with negligible decoding-speed overhead. The code is available at https://github.com/cindy2000sh/v-steer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes V-Steer, an inference-time method to enforce instruction hierarchies in LLMs by editing cached value vectors, greatly improving compliance with higher-priority prompts without retraining or major speed costs.
AI.motivation: In practice, large language models often fail to respect the intended instruction hierarchy where system prompts or higher-priority instructions should override conflicting user or tool instructions. This is a core safety and reliability assumption in deployment, and its violation undermines control over model behavior. Existing training-based methods to fix this can be costly and model-specific, while prompt-only techniques are often insufficient. The paper is motivated by the need for a training-free, efficient, and robust mechanism to restore privileged influence of high-priority prompts during inference.
AI.method: The authors introduce V-Steer, a training-free, inference-time intervention that operates on cached value (V) vectors in the transformer’s attention mechanism. First, they perform direct logit attribution on the first next-token prediction to identify attention heads where lower-priority spans (e.g., user instructions) exert more influence than privileged spans (e.g., system prompts). Once such heads are identified, they apply in-place multiplicative edits to the cached V tensors: boosting contributions from privileged spans while suppressing conflicting lower-priority spans. Because this operates only on cached values during prefill, it remains compatible with fused attention backends and adds only a one-time prefill overhead, leaving decoding speed nearly unchanged.
AI.result: On controlled role-conflict benchmarks across models ranging from 7B to 70B parameters, V-Steer increases primary constraint accuracy from below 18% to as high as 92%. On broader instruction hierarchy evaluations, it substantially outperforms prompt-only baselines and matches or surpasses state-of-the-art training-based approaches on three of four model scales. These performance gains are achieved with negligible impact on decoding speed due to the lightweight, prefill-only intervention.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that V-Steer is an effective and practical method to restore instruction hierarchies in LLMs at inference time without additional training. By targeting cached value vectors in specific attention heads identified through direct logit attribution, it can substantially increase adherence to higher-priority constraints while preserving efficiency and compatibility with standard inference backends. This demonstrates that structured, attribution-guided edits to internal representations can offer a powerful tool for improving controllability and safety properties of large language models.

title: ClinLens: Towards Long-Horizon Coding Agents for Longitudinal Multimodal Clinical Data Science
summary: Clinical data-science agents must transform heterogeneous longitudinal records into auditable analyses, yet existing benchmarks largely isolate medical question answering, structured-table reasoning, or generic scientific repositories. We introduce CLINLENS, a benchmark of 200 executable tasks over five linked MIMIC resources spanning structured electronic health records, notes, electrocardiograms, chest radiographs, and echocardiograms. A 4 x 5 taxonomy crosses four patient-time scopes with five analysis capabilities. Program-first reverse synthesis pairs each bounded semi-raw package with an evaluator-private reference workflow and checks required artifacts, cohort and temporal semantics, and the final answer. On a fixed 126-task suite, the strongest of 24 standardized model-scaffold configurations achieves 56.3% scope-macro STRICTPASS despite 100% EXECSUCCESS. For reference, a separately configured coding agent solves 83 of 126 tasks, while five biomedical systems adapted to GPT-4o-mini reach at most 2.9% scope-macro STRICTPASS. These results expose a substantial gap between runnable submissions and correct clinical analyses.

AI.tldr: Introduces CLINLENS, a benchmark for clinical data-science agents combining multiple MIMIC data sources to evaluate realistic, auditable longitudinal analyses, revealing a large gap between code that runs and clinically correct analyses.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus narrowly on single skills like medical QA or table reasoning and do not reflect the real-world challenge: transforming heterogeneous, longitudinal clinical records into auditable analyses across multiple modalities and time scopes. There is a need for a benchmark that captures the complexity of clinical data-science workflows and can rigorously evaluate agents' abilities to produce correct, well-scoped, temporally coherent analyses, not just executable code.
AI.method: They construct CLINLENS, a benchmark of 200 executable tasks over five linked MIMIC resources (structured EHRs, clinical notes, ECGs, chest radiographs, echocardiograms). They define a 4x5 taxonomy combining four patient-time scopes with five analysis capabilities. For each task, they use a program-first reverse synthesis approach: each semi-raw data package is paired with an evaluator-private reference workflow. Submissions are evaluated via automated checks on required artifacts, cohort and temporal semantics, and final answers. They also instantiate 24 standardized LLM+tool scaffolds and a separate coding agent, and adapt five existing biomedical systems to the benchmark, measuring performance using metrics like EXECSUCCESS and scope-macro STRICTPASS.
AI.result: On a 126-task subset, the best of 24 model-scaffold configurations achieves 56.3% scope-macro STRICTPASS while attaining 100% EXECSUCCESS, indicating that all generated programs run but many are semantically or clinically incorrect. A separate, more specialized coding agent correctly solves 83 of 126 tasks. In contrast, five biomedical systems adapted to GPT-4o-mini perform poorly, with a maximum of 2.9% scope-macro STRICTPASS. This highlights sizeable performance gaps across systems and between execution success and analytic correctness.
AI.conclusion: CLINLENS provides a realistic, multi-modal, longitudinal benchmark for evaluating clinical data-science agents, with rigorous, program-based evaluation of cohort selection, temporal reasoning, and analytic outputs. Initial results show that current general-purpose and biomedical systems often produce runnable but clinically incorrect analyses, underscoring the need for better models, tools, and scaffolding to achieve reliable, auditable clinical data science in practice.

title: A large-scale corpus of religious radio broadcast transcripts from webstream recordings in the United States
summary: Religious radio is a widespread but understudied form of mass communication in the United States, and content-level analysis of it has been constrained by the absence of large-scale transcript data. This Data Descriptor presents a corpus of transcribed English-language religious radio broadcasts captured from live webstreams over a one-month period in July 2025. Fifteen-minute segments were recorded on a rolling schedule from 785 distinct streams, which together rebroadcast the signals of more than two thousand AM and FM stations, yielding over 700,000 recordings and more than 60 million diarized lines of speech. Each recording was transcribed and speaker-diarized with an automated pipeline, and segmented and labeled by programming format and topic using a large language model. The corpus is organized as linked tables of stream metadata, recording metadata, and transcript lines. It supports descriptive study of religious broadcasting across regions and traditions, analysis of how social and political issues are discussed in religious media, and speech-processing research in an underrepresented domain.

AI.tldr: Creates a large, structured transcript corpus of U.S. religious radio broadcasts for research use.
AI.motivation: Religious radio is common in the U.S. but has been little studied because large-scale, structured transcripts have not been available. This limits quantitative and qualitative research on its content, including how it addresses social issues, and also deprives speech-technology of data from this domain.
AI.method: Over one month (July 2025), the authors continuously sampled 15-minute segments from 785 English-language religious radio webstreams that rebroadcast over 2,000 AM/FM stations. They automatically recorded, transcribed, and speaker-diarized more than 700,000 audio segments, then used a large language model to segment and label each recording by programming format and topic. The final dataset is stored as interlinked tables capturing stream metadata, recording metadata, and diarized transcript lines.
AI.result: The project produced a corpus containing over 700,000 recordings and more than 60 million diarized lines of speech, each linked to rich metadata and annotated with program formats and topical labels. This creates a structured, queryable dataset that covers a broad cross-section of U.S. religious radio content over the collection period.
AI.conclusion: This corpus enables large-scale empirical study of religious radio, including comparisons across regions and traditions and examination of how social and political topics are framed in religious media. It also offers a substantial, previously underrepresented resource for speech-processing research, helping to improve models on religious and conversational broadcast audio.

title: When benchmark inferences do not compose: Projectibility in AI evaluation
comment: 35 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Substantially rewritten and retitled; supersedes arXiv:2510.15236, whose homeostatic property-cluster account and proposed centrality-prior and cluster-stability measures are withdrawn. The argument, apparatus, and empirical companion are new. Code and empirical companion: https://github.com/BrettRey/benchmark-inference-composition
summary: An AI benchmark result rarely reaches a consequential claim in one step. Evaluators generalize it to further cases, interpret it as evidence of capability, extrapolate it to new tasks, transport it to another system or site, and combine it with assumptions about human review and downstream consequences. Validity-centred approaches require evidence for each claim. This paper identifies a further epistemic problem: warranted links don't automatically make a warranted chain. The target of one study may not be the source of the next; system, population, outcome, or conditions may change at the interface; and shared data or model lineage may make apparently independent support dependent. Projectibility concerns whether a bounded extension from observed to unobserved cases is warranted. Goodman supplies the problem of rival extensions; argument-based validity supplies an architecture for testing them. The paper's distinctive claim is a non-composition principle: support for adjacent projections warrants their composition only when endpoints and assumptions align and dependence and uncertainty are carried through. A legal-research case shows how benchmark evidence and a deployment study can each be sound while remaining parallel. A reanalysis and simulation show why aggregate stability can erase distinctions a later projection requires. The resulting projectibility audit diagnoses unsupported joins in benchmark-to-use arguments.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI benchmark results often get overstretched into broad claims through chains of inferences, and it proposes a “projectibility audit” method to check where those chains stop being justified.
AI.motivation: AI benchmarks are frequently treated as strong evidence about real-world performance, safety, and downstream impact. However, moving from a benchmark score to claims about deployment involves many intermediate generalizations (to other data, tasks, systems, settings, and human–AI interactions). Validity-centered approaches typically examine each step in isolation but overlook whether individually reasonable steps compose into a justified overall argument. The authors aim to expose this gap and provide a way to assess when benchmark-based claims about use are or are not warranted.
AI.method: Conceptual and methodological analysis building on Goodman's notion of projectibility and argument-based validity theory. The authors define different types of “links” that connect benchmark results to broader claims (changes in system, population, outcome, conditions, and dependencies in data/model lineage). They then formulate a non-composition principle specifying when local support between adjacent steps does not guarantee global support for the full chain. They illustrate the framework with (1) a legal-research AI case study comparing benchmark evidence and a deployment study, and (2) a reanalysis plus simulation that show how aggregate metrics can hide important differences required for later projections. Finally, they formalize these ideas into a structured “projectibility audit” procedure.
AI.result: The analysis shows that even when each individual study or inference step appears valid, chaining them can yield unjustified benchmark-to-use conclusions if assumptions, endpoints, or dependencies shift or remain implicit. The legal-research case demonstrates that benchmark evaluations and deployment studies can each be methodologically sound yet fail to support each other’s conclusions because they concern different targets or conditions. The reanalysis and simulations reveal that stable aggregate performance across conditions can mask divergences that become critical when making further projections. From these observations, the authors derive concrete diagnostic checks for where projections between studies fail (e.g., misaligned populations, outcomes, system versions, or unaccounted data/model dependencies).
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that validity evidence for AI benchmarks must be assessed not only link-by-link but also at the level of whole argument chains from benchmark to use. Local projectibility does not, by itself, guarantee global projectibility. To avoid overclaiming from benchmark results, evaluators should apply a projectibility audit that (1) makes endpoints and assumptions explicit, (2) tracks changes in systems, populations, outcomes, and conditions between studies, and (3) carries forward uncertainties and dependencies. Only when these factors align can adjacent projections legitimately compose into warranted claims about real-world deployment.

title: Robostreet Flow: A Lightweight, Ultra-Low-Drag Electric Tractor and Four-Truck Hybrid Convoy Architecture for Minimum-Cost Point-to-Point Freight
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems 2026
summary: Line-haul trucking costs are dominated by three comparably sized components: energy, driver labor, and equipment. Most efficiency technologies address only one component at a time. This paper presents Robostreet Flow, a freight architecture that jointly optimizes the vehicle, convoy formation, and operating model to minimize cost per ton-mile on high-volume point-to-point corridors. The Flow platform is a battery-electric 6x4 tractor with a teardrop single-seat cab and a drag coefficient of 0.35, approximately 40% below that of conventional Class 8 tractors. A carbon-composite monocoque and structurally integrated batteries reduce net vehicle weight by 50%. A 513 kWh tractor battery and a 340 kWh powered trailer battery provide a 500-mile single-charge range. Four Flow trucks operate as a coordinated convoy with a safety driver only in the lead vehicle, while three followers operate in SAE Level 4 automated mode. Computational fluid dynamics simulations show that close following at an 8 m gap reduces follower drag coefficients by 42-48% and follower peak frontal pressure by approximately a factor of four relative to the exposed lead vehicle. A longitudinal energy model calibrated to these results predicts fleet-average consumption of 1.27 kWh/mi in convoy, compared with 1.60 kWh/mi for an isolated vehicle, for a 20.5% energy saving. Electricity cost is approximately 17% of the equivalent diesel fuel cost. Amortizing one driver across four trucks and accounting for the additional payload enabled by lightweighting reduce operating cost from 9.4 to 4.1 cents per ton-mile, a 56% reduction relative to a diesel baseline. Sensitivity analysis, a hub-to-hub operating concept, and regulatory implications are also presented.

AI.tldr: Proposes an integrated electric truck and convoy system (“Robostreet Flow”) that uses highly aerodynamic, lightweight vehicles and partially automated platooning to cut long-haul freight cost and energy use per ton‑mile by roughly half versus diesel.
AI.motivation: Line‑haul trucking costs are largely driven by energy, driver wages, and equipment, each contributing comparably. Existing efficiency measures tend to optimize only one of these factors, leaving substantial system‑level savings untapped. There is a need for a holistic freight architecture that simultaneously addresses vehicle design, energy use, automation, and operating model to significantly reduce cost per ton‑mile and improve energy efficiency on high‑volume freight corridors.
AI.method: The authors design a new freight architecture called Robostreet Flow, centered on a battery‑electric Class 8 tractor–trailer platform and a convoy operating concept. They specify a highly aerodynamic 6x4 tractor with a teardrop single‑seat cab and low drag coefficient, lightweight carbon‑composite monocoque construction with structurally integrated batteries, and dual battery packs on tractor and powered trailer sized for 500‑mile range. They then model a four‑truck convoy in which only the lead vehicle has a safety driver and the three followers operate at SAE Level 4 automation with tight following distances. Using computational fluid dynamics, they quantify aerodynamic drag and pressure reductions for followers at an 8 m gap, and calibrate a longitudinal energy model with these results to estimate energy consumption in convoy versus solo operation. Finally, they perform cost and payload calculations and a sensitivity analysis comparing against a diesel baseline; they also discuss hub‑to‑hub operations and regulatory aspects conceptually.
AI.result: CFD simulations indicate that with an 8 m following distance, follower trucks experience 42–48% reductions in drag coefficient and roughly fourfold reductions in peak frontal pressure compared to the lead vehicle. The calibrated energy model predicts that, in convoy, average fleet consumption is 1.27 kWh/mi versus 1.60 kWh/mi for an isolated Flow truck, giving a 20.5% energy saving from platooning. The electric energy cost is estimated to be about 17% of the cost of equivalent diesel fuel. The proposed lightweight, aerodynamic vehicle, combined with dual battery packs providing a 500‑mile range and a four‑truck convoy with one human driver, reduces operating cost from 9.4 to 4.1 cents per ton‑mile, a 56% reduction relative to a conventional diesel baseline. Additional payload from lower vehicle weight further boosts economic performance.
AI.conclusion: An integrated approach that co‑optimizes vehicle design, electrification, platooning, and operating model can dramatically cut both energy use and cost in long‑haul freight. The Robostreet Flow concept demonstrates that a purpose‑built, lightweight, battery‑electric tractor with a powered trailer, operated in partially automated four‑truck convoys with a single safety driver, can reduce energy consumption by about one‑fifth and total operating cost per ton‑mile by more than half compared with conventional diesel trucking. The work suggests that hub‑to‑hub convoy operations, if supported by suitable regulations and infrastructure, could unlock substantial economic and environmental gains in high‑volume freight corridors.

title: GuideSkill: Evolving Executable LLM Agent Skills for Guideline-Grounded Clinical Reasoning
summary: Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) encode diagnostic criteria, but LLM systems typically retrieve guideline text or absorb it through training rather than execute its rules. We introduce GuideSkill, an external reasoning layer that compiles disease-specific criteria into executable functions returning ordinal diagnostic-support scores. GuideSkill-Zero is initialized from guidelines, while GuideSkill-Evo uses case--diagnosis pairs to refine covered skills and add missing diagnoses. At inference, an LLM proposes a differential diagnosis, grounds the features required by each matched skill, and fuses its ranking with the executed skill scores. Across four benchmarks and four backbones, GuideSkill-Zero improves macro-average accuracy over guideline RAG by 13.45% on average. GuideSkill-Evo achieves the highest macro-average for every backbone, improves over direct inference by 18.49% relatively, and increases gold-label skill coverage from 56.5% to 99.5%. On Qwen3.5-9B, it also exceeds the strongest parameter-update baseline by 11.16% without updating the backbone. Expert evaluation further indicates that GuideSkill produces clinically sound and broadly acceptable skills, suggesting that its initialized and evolved rules are reliable and practically meaningful. These results support executable skills as a model-agnostic mechanism for combining guideline-derived procedures with case-derived diagnostic patterns.

AI.tldr: GuideSkill is an external, executable reasoning layer that turns clinical guideline rules into functions, which, combined with LLM reasoning, significantly improves diagnostic accuracy without retraining the base model.
AI.motivation: LLMs currently handle clinical practice guidelines mostly by retrieving or memorizing text instead of explicitly executing guideline logic, limiting reliability, transparency, and alignment with formal diagnostic criteria. The authors want a way to make models follow guideline-style rules while also benefiting from data-driven diagnostic patterns.
AI.method: They design GuideSkill, a model-agnostic reasoning layer that compiles disease-specific diagnostic criteria from clinical guidelines into executable skills that output ordinal diagnostic-support scores. Two variants are proposed: GuideSkill-Zero, initialized directly from guideline criteria, and GuideSkill-Evo, which further refines and expands skills using case–diagnosis data. At inference, an LLM generates a differential diagnosis, identifies and grounds patient features for each relevant skill, and its ranking is then combined with the scores from executing the skills to produce final predictions.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and four different LLM backbones, GuideSkill-Zero outperforms guideline-based retrieval-augmented generation by an average of 13.45% in macro-average accuracy. GuideSkill-Evo consistently achieves the best macro-average performance for every backbone, with an 18.49% relative gain over direct LLM inference, raises coverage of gold-label skills from 56.5% to 99.5%, and, on Qwen3.5-9B, beats the strongest parameter-updated baseline by 11.16% without modifying the backbone parameters.
AI.conclusion: Executable skills derived from clinical guidelines and refined with case data provide a robust, interpretable, and model-agnostic way to integrate formal guideline procedures with empirical diagnostic patterns, yielding clinically sound, reliable, and substantially more accurate diagnostic support without retraining the underlying LLM.

title: Evaluating Prompt Scope and Demonstration Similarity in Local LLM Machine Translation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as general-purpose translation systems, but their behavior is usually evaluated under a single prompt shape: translate one source sentence into one target language. In practice, users may ask for one target language, for several related languages at once, or for translations conditioned on examples. This paper studies prompt scope and demonstration selection as experimental variables for local LLM machine translation. We evaluate English-to-Romance and English-to-Germanic translation on the full FLORES devtest split for nine official European Union languages. We compare three local instruction-tuned LLMs, llama3.2:3b, mistral:latest, and qwen2.5:14b, against dedicated MT baselines from OPUS-MT and NLLB-200. We test zero-shot prompting and k=5 few-shot prompting with random, lexical-similarity, and embedding-similarity demonstration selection. We also compare single-target prompts with JSON-formatted family-scope prompts that request all languages in a family at once. Results show that dedicated MT systems remain strongest overall, especially for Germanic languages. Few-shot prompting helps mistral:latest and qwen2.5:14b, but hurts llama3.2:3b; embedding retrieval is best on average for the stronger LLMs, but its advantage over random and lexical examples is modest. Family-scope prompting is feasible for stronger local LLMs but exposes structured-output failures in smaller models. These findings motivate evaluating LLM translation not only by language pair and metric, but also by prompt scope, retrieval strategy, and multi-target compliance.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how different prompt designs and example-selection strategies affect the translation quality of local LLMs, compared against strong MT baselines, across multiple European languages.
AI.motivation: LLMs are widely used as general-purpose translators, but most evaluations only consider a narrow, single-sentence, single-target-language prompt. Real users issue more complex requests, such as translating into multiple related languages at once or conditioning on examples. There is a need to understand how prompt scope and demonstration selection influence LLM translation quality in realistic local settings and how they compare to specialized MT systems.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three local instruction-tuned LLMs (llama3.2:3b, mistral:latest, qwen2.5:14b) on English-to-Romance and English-to-Germanic translation using the FLORES devtest split for nine EU languages. They compare these models with dedicated MT baselines (OPUS-MT and NLLB-200). They run experiments in zero-shot and k=5 few-shot settings, where few-shot demonstrations are chosen by three strategies: random selection, lexical similarity, and embedding-based similarity. They also compare single-target prompts against JSON-formatted family-scope prompts that request translations into all languages of a family at once, and they assess translation quality and structured-output fidelity under these different conditions.
AI.result: Dedicated MT systems outperform the local LLMs overall, particularly for Germanic languages. Few-shot prompting improves the performance of mistral:latest and qwen2.5:14b but degrades performance for llama3.2:3b. For the stronger LLMs, embedding-based demonstration retrieval gives the best average gains, though its advantage over random or lexical-based selection is relatively small. Family-scope JSON prompting works reasonably well for the stronger local LLMs but leads to more structured-output failures for smaller models.
AI.conclusion: Specialized MT models still hold a performance edge over local LLMs in this setup, but LLM translation performance is sensitive to prompt scope and demonstration strategy. Evaluations of LLM-based MT should therefore go beyond simple single-target, zero-shot settings and explicitly consider prompt design (including multi-language family-scope prompts), retrieval strategy for examples, and models’ ability to follow structured multi-target output requirements.

title: GoGoTB: Agentic RTL Verification with Specification-Grounded Coverage Closure
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Xin Xin and Jincheng Lou contributed equally to this work and share first authorship
summary: Functional verification dominates integrated circuit (IC) front-end engineering effort, and a single missed bug that escapes to silicon can trigger a costly respin. Recent large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to automate this process, yet existing LLM-based approaches generate each component through independent single-turn calls with no shared context, leaving interface mismatches undetected and reported coverage disconnected from specification requirements. To address these challenges, we present GoGoTB, an agentic framework that achieves end-to-end verification closure through three subsystems: an agentic execution control layer, an evolvable knowledge system, and specification-grounded coverage closure. The execution control layer separates deterministic enforcement from LLM reasoning at every tool and stage boundary. The knowledge system dispatches methodology and design-specific expertise on demand. The coverage framework anchors every bin to a named specification behavior so that each residual gap has a diagnosable root cause and a targeted remedy. Tested on 8 register transfer level (RTL) designs without any human intervention, GoGoTB achieves 100\% environment generation success and averages 98.4\% line, 97.2\% branch, 97.0\% toggle, and 83.2\% functional coverage. No prior work successfully generates a complete verification environment or achieves meaningful coverage on the same benchmarks.

AI.tldr: GoGoTB is an LLM-driven, agentic verification framework that automatically builds complete IC verification environments and closes coverage, achieving near-human coverage metrics without human intervention.
AI.motivation: Functional verification is the dominant cost in IC front-end design, and missed bugs can cause expensive silicon respins. Existing LLM-based verification approaches treat tasks as isolated, single-turn generations with no shared context, leading to interface mismatches and coverage that is not traceable to the specification. There is a need for a system that can coordinate LLM reasoning, maintain evolving design knowledge, and connect coverage directly to spec behaviors to achieve end-to-end, automated verification closure.
AI.method: The paper proposes GoGoTB, an agentic framework for RTL verification consisting of three coordinated subsystems: (1) an agentic execution control layer that cleanly separates deterministic enforcement (tools, scripts, constraints) from LLM-based reasoning at every boundary; (2) an evolvable knowledge system that stores and dispatches methodology- and design-specific expertise on demand to guide the LLM; and (3) a specification-grounded coverage framework that ties every coverage bin to an explicit named spec behavior, enabling diagnosis of residual coverage gaps and targeted fixes. GoGoTB orchestrates these components to automatically generate verification environments and drive coverage closure.
AI.result: On 8 RTL designs, and without any human intervention, GoGoTB achieves 100% success in generating complete verification environments. It reaches on average 98.4% line coverage, 97.2% branch coverage, 97.0% toggle coverage, and 83.2% functional coverage. Prior LLM-based work on the same benchmarks fails to generate full environments and does not reach meaningful coverage levels, highlighting GoGoTB’s superior automation and effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: GoGoTB demonstrates that an agentic, context-aware LLM framework with structured execution control, a shared knowledge base, and spec-anchored coverage can automatically achieve near-closure in RTL functional verification. This suggests that LLMs, when properly orchestrated rather than used as isolated single-turn generators, can substantially reduce human effort in IC verification and improve traceability from specification to coverage, surpassing previous LLM-based approaches on standard benchmarks.

title: AgentGUI: An Interface for Observing and Steering Long-Running AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly adept at tackling complex, long-running tasks. With the rapid surge of autonomous capabilities, human oversight is systematically lagging behind due to limited human-centered interfacing. Aiming to address this, we introduce AgentGUI, a user-friendly, locally hosted GUI for seamlessly observing and steering AI agents amid multiple concurrent, long-running sessions. AgentGUI features 1) rich agent trajectory visualizations, 2) effective manual and automated steering, and 3) integration with and coordination between open-source and frontier agent frameworks. A controlled user study demonstrates statistically significant reduction in the time it takes to identify key elements from agent traces (38% faster, p = 0.023). In a preliminary experiment, AgentGUI's automated drift prevention feature raises the task completion rate of small local agents by as high as 34pp across a 0.8B--9B model ladder (N=50 runs per model). AgentGUI is publicly available through its project website (https://agent-gui-project.github.io) and open-source repository (https://github.com/eth-medical-ai-lab/agent-gui), along with a demo video (https://youtube.com/watch?v=GSDyxN1gTF0).

AI.tldr: AgentGUI is a local, user-friendly interface to observe, visualize, and steer multiple long-running AI agents, improving oversight efficiency and preventing drift.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become more autonomous and handle complex, long-duration tasks, human oversight struggles to keep up because existing interfaces are not sufficiently human-centered, making it hard to monitor, understand, and control agents across concurrent sessions.
AI.method: The authors design and implement AgentGUI, a locally hosted graphical interface that connects to various agent frameworks. It provides detailed visualizations of agent trajectories, tools for manual and automated steering (including drift prevention), and mechanisms to integrate and coordinate different agent systems. They then conduct a controlled user study measuring how fast users can identify key elements in agent traces, and a preliminary experiment evaluating automated drift prevention across models of different sizes.
AI.result: In the user study, participants using AgentGUI identified key elements from agent traces 38% faster than a baseline (p = 0.023). In the drift prevention experiment, AgentGUI’s automated steering feature increased task completion rates of smaller local agents by up to 34 percentage points across models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, with 50 runs per model.
AI.conclusion: AgentGUI effectively enhances human oversight of autonomous AI agents by improving trace comprehension speed and boosting task completion through automated drift prevention. It serves as a practical, open-source tool for monitoring and steering multiple agent frameworks, supporting safer and more efficient deployment of long-running AI agents.

title: Position: Evaluation Scores Are Perishable Knowledge Claims
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Published at the Fifth Workshop on Generation, Evaluation and Metrics (GEM), ACL 2026, San Diego
summary: Evaluation methodologies for language models increasingly combine multiple signals, from automated metrics and LLM-as-judge ratings to human assessments and benchmark suite results. When these signals are aggregated via averaging, evaluation confidence can then substantially exceed the reliability of the weakest signal: a phenomenon we call trust inflation in evaluation. We argue that evaluation scores should be treated as epistemic claims with three properties: formality (human evaluation provides stronger evidence than an automated metric), scope (a benchmark result applies to the tested distribution, not universally), and validity windows (benchmark results expire as contamination accumulates and distributions shift). Several converging research traditions (chain-of-thought analysis, possibilistic logic, and algebraic theory) establish weakest-link aggregation as the conservative endpoint of a parameterized operator family controlled by a single pessimism parameter. Drawing on those traditions, and on concrete lessons from building an evaluation harness for agentic AI, we propose that evaluation results carry explicit metadata (formality tier, scope declaration, and expiration date) to make their epistemic status transparent. We illustrate the cost of mean aggregation on the public HELM leaderboard: across 54 frontier models on ten scenarios, the top-five models ranked by mean score and by weakest-link are completely disjoint.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques standard practice of averaging heterogeneous evaluation signals for language models, showing this causes misleading overconfidence (‘trust inflation’), and proposes a weakest-link-based aggregation plus explicit metadata about each score’s reliability, scope, and validity period.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation pipelines combine many different signals (automatic metrics, LLM-judges, human studies, benchmarks) and typically average them into single scores or leaderboards. This hides differences in reliability, domain coverage, and obsolescence of benchmarks, leading to overconfident and potentially wrong conclusions about model quality. The authors want a more epistemically sound way to interpret and aggregate evaluation results so that performance claims match the actual strength and limits of the evidence.
AI.method: Conceptually, they reinterpret evaluation scores as epistemic claims characterized by three dimensions: (1) formality – how strong the evidence is (e.g., human studies vs. automated metrics), (2) scope – what data distribution or use case the result applies to, and (3) validity window – how long the result can be trusted before contamination or distribution shift undermines it. Mathematically and logically, they connect to prior work in chain-of-thought analysis, possibilistic logic, and algebraic theory to justify a family of aggregation operators parameterized by a pessimism level, where standard mean is optimistic and a weakest-link operator is maximally conservative. Empirically, they examine the public HELM leaderboard, comparing rankings produced with mean aggregation versus weakest-link aggregation across 54 models and ten scenarios.
AI.result: They show that averaging evaluation signals can greatly inflate apparent confidence: evaluation scores may look robust even when some component signals are weak or unreliable. In their HELM case study, the top-five models under mean aggregation and under weakest-link aggregation do not overlap at all, demonstrating that aggregation choice drastically changes perceived model ranking. Their theoretical framing positions weakest-link aggregation as the conservative endpoint in a continuum of epistemic attitudes. They also specify a practical metadata schema for evaluation reports, including a formality tier, explicit scope declaration, and an expiration date for each result.
AI.conclusion: Mean-based aggregation of heterogeneous evaluation signals leads to “trust inflation” and can misrepresent how well language models are actually understood or compared. A more principled approach is to treat evaluation results as constrained epistemic claims, annotate them with structured metadata about evidence strength, scope, and validity duration, and to aggregate signals using operators that respect the weakest evidence rather than diluting it via averaging. This yields more transparent, conservative, and trustworthy evaluations and shows that current leaderboards may be substantially misranking models due to overly optimistic aggregation methods.

title: When Synthetic Users Fail: A Cross-Domain Benchmark of LLM-Simulated Human Survey Responses
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Preprint; under review
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic users, stand-ins for human respondents whose simulated answers feed product, policy, and market decisions. We ask when this substitution is valid and when it fails, and package the answer as an evaluation framework for intelligent synthetic-user systems. A single protocol, run across four models spanning two families and an 8B-to-frontier capability range, is applied to two independent domains of real human-response data: U.S. general social attitudes (General Social Survey) and cross-cultural values (World Values Survey). Every model is benchmarked against a suite of non-LLM baselines fit on held-out human data. Under demographic prompting and the survey-simulation protocols we test, two failures replicate across both domains, all four models, and both families. First, at the individual level no LLM beats even the strongest baseline; on cross-cultural values every model falls well below it, and the gap survives distance-aware and proper scoring. Second, models systematically over-determine demographics, treating identity as far more predictive of attitudes than it is among real people, a distortion present for nearly every question-group combination and robust to a coding-invariant measure. Neither failure is remedied by a larger, more capable model. A decision-impact analysis shows why this matters in practice: on a segment-targeting task the models inflate between-segment gaps two to fourfold, would direct a team to the wrong segment in half of U.S. and most cross-cultural cases, and manufacture segment splits that do not exist in real people. We make the cross-domain benchmark and the evaluation framework available on request, so that teams can determine in advance when synthetic-user evidence is safe for decision support and when it is not.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates when large language models can validly act as synthetic survey respondents and finds systematic, robust failures that limit their safe use for decision-making.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as cheap, fast substitutes for human survey respondents in product, policy, and market research, but it is unclear under what conditions their responses faithfully approximate real human attitudes and segments. Miscalibrated trust in synthetic users could distort decisions, so a principled evaluation is needed.
AI.method: The authors design a unified evaluation protocol for ".synthetic-user" systems and apply it to four LLMs from two model families, ranging from 8B to frontier scale. They simulate survey responses under demographic prompting across two independent, real human-response datasets: the U.S. General Social Survey and the cross-national World Values Survey. For each model, they compare individual-level predictive performance against a suite of non-LLM baselines trained on held-out human data, assess how strongly models treat demographics as predictors of attitudes (using coding-invariant, distance-aware, and proper scoring measures), and run a decision-impact analysis on segment-targeting tasks.
AI.result: Across both domains, all four models, and both families, two key failure modes emerge. (1) At the individual level, no LLM outperforms the strongest non-LLM baseline; on cross-cultural values, every model performs substantially worse, and this deficit remains under distance-aware and proper scoring evaluations. (2) LLMs systematically over-attribute predictive power to demographic variables, treating identity (e.g., demographic segments) as much more determinative of attitudes than observed in real human data. This pattern appears for nearly every question-group pairing and is robust to different measurement choices. Scaling to larger, more capable models does not fix these problems. In a simulated segment-targeting decision task, these distortions cause the models to exaggerate between-segment differences by factors of two to four, frequently select the wrong target segment in about half of U.S. cases and most cross-cultural cases, and even fabricate segment splits that do not exist in real data.
AI.conclusion: Using current LLMs as synthetic survey respondents is often invalid for fine-grained, individual-level prediction and segment-based decision-making, because they underperform standard baselines and systematically exaggerate the causal role of demographics. These biases persist across models, domains, and evaluation metrics, and are not alleviated by greater scale. The authors propose and release a cross-domain benchmark and evaluation framework so practitioners can rigorously test synthetic-user setups before relying on them for decision support, identifying when such evidence is trustworthy and when it risks misleading decisions.

title: TraceCoder: Explainable and Auditable Code Generation with Position-Key Snippet Versioning
comment: Submitted Version (version submitted on May deadline to AGENTICS 2026). Version of Record to appear in AGENTICS proceedings
summary: Contemporary LLM-based coding agents produce code as black-box outputs: the rationale behind each line is hidden, the evolution of the code through benchmark-driven repair is ephemeral, and post-hoc auditing is impossible. We present a code generation concept that addresses these shortcomings through three complementary mechanisms: (i) a relational snippet-history schema that records, per repair event, the benchmark reference, round number, failure text, and LLM explanation, enabling full provenance queries; (ii) a browser-based visualisation tool that renders this history as heat-mapped, hover-annotated source code; and (iii) a competitive fractional position-key indexing scheme with tree-node delimiters that assigns stable, lexicographically-ordered identifiers to each code snippet, enabling fine-grained tracking without disrupting surrounding lines. We evaluate TraceCoder on 30 algorithmic programming tasks spanning string processing, mathematical computation, and data-structure manipulation, across two provider configurations. Of these, 10 exhaust the 6-iteration budget on tasks with subtle edge-case behaviour. Mean Chg% reaches 30%, three in ten code snippets carry a traceable repair-event row, compared to 21% when using Gemini 2.0 Flash as sole provider on a 20-task subset. Three detailed case studies demonstrate how the system explains which specific benchmark failures shaped each line of the final program. The proposed mechanism makes the internal "narrative" of automated code generation auditable and replayable, a property essential for trust and accountability in production deployments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TraceCoder, a system that makes LLM-based code generation transparent and auditable by recording and visualizing the full history of code repairs and their benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based coding agents generate code as black boxes, hiding the reasoning behind each line, the iterative repair process, and making later auditing impossible. This lack of transparency undermines trust and accountability, especially in production settings where one must understand why code looks the way it does and how test failures influenced it.
AI.method: The authors design three main mechanisms: (1) a relational snippet-history schema that logs, for every repair event, the triggering benchmark, iteration number, failure description, and LLM explanation to support provenance queries; (2) a browser visualization that overlays this history on the source code with heatmaps and hover annotations; and (3) a fractional position-key indexing scheme with tree-node delimiters that gives each code snippet a stable, lexicographically ordered identifier, enabling precise tracking through edits without disturbing surrounding lines. They implement these components in a system called TraceCoder and use it with different LLM provider configurations on programming benchmarks.
AI.result: On 30 algorithmic tasks (string, math, data structures) and two LLM provider setups, 10 tasks fully consume the 6-iteration repair budget due to subtle edge cases. The system achieves a mean change percentage of 30%, and about 30% of code snippets are linked to at least one repair-event record, versus 21% when using only Gemini 2.0 Flash on a 20-task subset. Case studies show that TraceCoder can pinpoint which benchmark failures led to specific lines in the final code.
AI.conclusion: TraceCoder provides a practical way to expose the internal "narrative" of LLM-driven code generation, making each line’s evolution traceable to concrete benchmark failures and explanations. This transforms code generation from an opaque process into one that is auditable and replayable, which the authors argue is a key requirement for deploying automated coding tools in trustworthy, accountable production environments.

title: Symphony of Bias: Exploring Gender Associations with Musical Instruments in Multimodal LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in everyday life and widely used for information seeking, raising concerns about their potential to perpetuate social biases and reinforce stereotypes. In this study, we investigate gender bias in LLMs through the lens of their associations with musical instruments. Building on social-science research on the cultural gender-typing of instruments, we introduce Symphony-Bias, a parallel multimodal dataset spanning text, vision, and audio. We evaluate ten multimodal models with diverse architectures and scales across 22 musical instruments, analyzing how they associate each instrument with three gender categories: {male, female, non-binary}, across three modalities: {text, vision, audio}. Our results show that 92\% of instrument-level outcomes align with prior social-science findings, with the harp and drums showing particularly consistent gendered associations across all evaluated models and modalities. We further find that alignment with social stereotypes is weakest in audio, stronger in vision, and strongest in text, suggesting that modality-specific representations can differentially amplify gendered associations with musical instruments.\footnote{The Symphony-Bias dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance of the paper.}

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Symphony-Bias, a multimodal dataset to measure gender bias in LLMs’ associations with musical instruments, and evaluates multiple models across text, vision, and audio.
