AI.motivation: Existing multimodal fake news detectors overfit to domain-specific shortcuts and spurious correlations caused by imbalanced datasets and semantically inconsistent text-image pairs. This leads to poor performance when applied to new domains or platforms, because the model has learned to rely on unreliable or non-generalizable patterns rather than robust cross-modal evidence. The authors aim to build a system that can better decide what evidence is trustworthy across domains and thus generalize more reliably.
AI.method: They propose Expert-Guided Mutual Distillation (EGMD), a framework that operates on three levels: (1) Input-level calibration: it measures and encodes the coherence between text and image for each pair as a shared gain factor before multimodal fusion, so cross-modal agreement/disagreement influences the input representation. (2) Representation-level expert guidance: a teacher network with expert modules is trained so that domain-specific patterns are captured in specialized experts and domain statistics are aligned across domains. (3) Decision-level mutual distillation: multiple domain-specific student models, anchored by prototypes, learn from each other and from the teacher through mutual learning and dual-channel distillation, inheriting the teacher's feature geometry and calibrated predictions while discouraging reliance on local domain priors. They also construct a new dataset, Weibo_Balanced, to control for domain imbalance.
AI.result: On four multimodal fake news datasets in two languages, EGMD achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and significantly reduces domain bias, with up to 57.3% reduction compared to baselines. The new Weibo_Balanced benchmark demonstrates that EGMD maintains strong performance even when domain imbalance is controlled, highlighting its improved cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that explicitly modeling which evidence to trust at input, representation, and decision levels enables multimodal fake news detectors to generalize better across domains. EGMD both improves detection accuracy and substantially reduces domain bias, and the proposed Weibo_Balanced dataset serves as a useful benchmark for analyzing the impact of domain imbalance on generalization in multimodal fake news detection.

title: AgenticCANN: Automated Ascend C Operator Generation via Knowledge-Augmented Agentic Evolution
summary: Ascend C operator optimization is critical for NPU (Neural Processing Unit) inference performance but requires deep hardware expertise.While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automated CUDA kernel generation, the fundamentally different programming model of Ascend C introduces unique challenges that remain unexplored. In this paper, we propose AgenticCANN, a knowledge-augmented agentic evolution framework specifically tailored for automated Ascend C operator synthesis in low-corpus NPU environments.To overcome the severe platform knowledge deficit on unfamiliar hardware, AgenticCANN incorporates a knowledge-orchestrated generation system that delivers structured, multi-level domain insights across the development lifecycle to resolve the upstream feasibility bottleneck.Building on this foundation, it features a stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy that dynamically aligns LLM interaction modes with specific generation and evolution phases, balancing high-exploration candidate discovery with high-convergence performance tuning.Extensive experiments on Huawei Ascend 910B across six operators spanning five pattern categories demonstrate that our method achieves 90 to 100 percent feasibility on elementwise and normalization operators, 56% on fusion operators, and up to 6.65$\times$ speedup on 1B Pangu model inference kernels. Further analysis reveals that knowledge injection monotonically improves feasibility from 57% to 86% on elementwise operators, demonstrating its general rather than operator-specific benefit.

AI.tldr: AgenticCANN is a knowledge-augmented agent framework that automatically generates and optimizes Ascend C operators for NPUs, achieving high feasibility and significant speedups with limited training corpus.
AI.motivation: Optimizing Ascend C operators is essential for NPU inference performance but currently demands deep, specialized hardware expertise. Existing LLM-based kernel generation methods mainly target CUDA and do not address Ascend C’s very different programming model or the low-availability of code/data on new NPUs. There is a need to systematically inject hardware and platform knowledge into LLMs and design an adaptive generation process that can work under these constraints and still produce feasible, high-performance kernels.
AI.method: The paper introduces AgenticCANN, a knowledge-augmented agentic evolution framework tailored for Ascend C. It uses a knowledge-orchestrated generation system that supplies structured, multi-level domain knowledge (about the hardware, programming model, and optimization practices) throughout the code development lifecycle to overcome platform knowledge gaps. On top of this, it employs a stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy: different LLM interaction modes and search behaviors are used for early-stage candidate exploration versus later-stage performance tuning, dynamically balancing exploration and convergence to iteratively synthesize and refine Ascend C operators.
AI.result: On Huawei Ascend 910B, evaluated across six operators from five pattern categories, AgenticCANN attains 90–100% feasibility on elementwise and normalization operators, 56% feasibility on fusion operators, and up to 6.65× speedup on 1B-parameter Pangu model inference kernels. Additional experiments show that progressively injecting more structured knowledge consistently improves feasibility on elementwise operators from 57% to 86%, suggesting broad effectiveness rather than narrow per-operator overfitting.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-augmented, agentic LLM frameworks like AgenticCANN can effectively automate Ascend C operator synthesis on NPUs even in low-corpus, low-familiarity settings. Structured domain knowledge injection and stage-adaptive evolution substantially improve both feasibility and performance, and the observed monotonic gains from knowledge injection indicate that the approach generalizes across operator types instead of relying on operator-specific tricks.

title: WikiLoop: Jointly Learning to Build and Navigate Agent-Native Wikis with Downstream Feedback
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 12 tables. Includes supplementary material
summary: Knowledge-base construction and querying are typically optimized in isolation: retrieval-augmented agents operate over a fixed, externally maintained index, whereas construction receives no signal from downstream use. We present WikiLoop, a feedback-coupled framework that jointly learns to build and navigate an agent-native Wiki, a persistent linked-page knowledge base designed for machine navigation. A role-conditioned shared policy supports two interfaces: a Navigator retrieves evidence from the Wiki to answer queries, and a Builder proposes structured edits evaluated through downstream navigation. The Navigator follows a sufficiency-before-efficiency objective that applies retrieval-cost penalties only after full evidence has been collected. The Builder learns from utility differences: a frozen Navigator scores each candidate edit by its change in downstream performance, while a guard penalty discourages regressions on unrelated queries. Training combines sequential role-specific optimization with a final joint stage over role-homogeneous batches. With Qwen3.5-9B as the common backbone, WikiLoop reaches 62.6 aggregate Answer Correctness on AuthTrace, 6.3 points above LLM-Wiki, base, with the largest gains on multi-document queries. Controlled comparisons support the intended effects of both objectives, and the learned edits remain useful to a held-out Navigator. Paired comparisons indicate that the final shared policy largely retains both role-specific capabilities, improves Navigator and end-to-end Answer Correctness by 0.4 points relative to the corresponding specialist references, and consolidates both interfaces into one model. Without dataset-specific training, WikiLoop also improves over the same-backbone LLM-Wiki, base on HotpotQA and MuSiQue.

AI.tldr: WikiLoop is a joint framework where an LLM both builds and uses its own wiki-style knowledge base, leading to better multi-document QA performance than prior LLM-Wiki baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented systems assume a fixed external index and do not let knowledge-base construction benefit from feedback from downstream query performance. This separation prevents the system from learning what kinds of pages, links, and edits are actually useful for answering queries efficiently and accurately. The authors want an agent-native, dynamically updated knowledge base where construction and navigation co-adapt based on end-task utility.
AI.method: They design WikiLoop, a persistent linked-page wiki tailored for machine navigation, and train a single shared, role-conditioned policy (on Qwen3.5-9B) that can act as either a Navigator or a Builder. The Navigator interacts with the wiki to gather evidence and answer questions under a ‘sufficiency-before-efficiency’ objective that penalizes retrieval cost only after sufficient evidence is gathered. The Builder proposes structured edits—creating or modifying pages and links—which are evaluated by a frozen Navigator that measures how each edit changes downstream QA performance. A guard penalty prevents hurting performance on unrelated queries. Training first optimizes each role separately on role-specific data, and then performs a joint finetuning stage on batches of examples where all instances share the same role, yielding a single policy that can switch roles via conditioning while largely retaining both skill sets.
AI.result: On the AuthTrace benchmark, WikiLoop with Qwen3.5-9B reaches 62.6 aggregate Answer Correctness, 6.3 points higher than the LLM-Wiki, base system, with especially strong gains on multi-document queries. Ablation-style, controlled comparisons confirm that the sufficiency-before-efficiency Navigator objective and the utility-difference-based Builder objective each contribute as intended. The edits learned during training still benefit a held-out Navigator model, showing that the constructed wiki has general utility. In paired evaluations, the final shared policy preserves most of the role-specific performance and improves Navigator and end-to-end Answer Correctness by about 0.4 points over specialist Navigator/Builder models, while unifying both interfaces in one model. WikiLoop also transfers without dataset-specific training to HotpotQA and MuSiQue, outperforming the same-backbone LLM-Wiki, base on these benchmarks as well.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning to build and navigate an agent-native wiki leads to better retrieval-augmented QA than treating indexing and retrieval as separate, fixed components. The sufficiency-before-efficiency navigation objective and the utility-difference-based editing objective enable the system to construct a knowledge base that is measurably more helpful for multi-hop and multi-document reasoning. A single shared, role-conditioned policy can effectively handle both navigation and construction, simplifying deployment while slightly improving QA accuracy over specialist models and generalizing to new datasets without task-specific retraining.

title: UrbanDS: A Graph-Guided LLM Multi-Agent System for Data-Intensive Urban Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have been widely applied in automating data science tasks. However, existing methods typically rely on a limited set of provided datasets, and they face challenges in data-intensive scenarios that require discovering and leveraging relevant information from large-scale and heterogeneous data repositories. Urban tasks are representative examples of such scenarios, as urban data are not only large-scale and multi-sourced, but also exhibit complex spatial, temporal, and semantic relationships. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanDS, a graph-guided LLM multi-agent system for data-intensive urban tasks. We first construct a unified dataset graph to organize reusable dataset skills and the relationships among datasets. Specifically, we develop a Data Profiling Agent that constructs a skill for each dataset. Moreover, a Relation Agent identifies relationships among datasets and integrates these relationships into the dataset graph. At runtime, a Planner Agent retrieves task-relevant datasets from the graph and generates execution plans. Multiple Execution Agents then perform data processing and analysis, while their execution progress and intermediate results are shared through a common memory. Finally, a Report Agent synthesizes the experimental logs into a report, which can be further refined based on user feedback. To systematically evaluate the capability of agents in handling data-intensive urban scenarios, we further construct UrbanDS-Bench, an urban data science benchmark covering representative data analysis and modeling tasks. Experiments on both general and urban benchmarks demonstrate that UrbanDS consistently outperforms existing data science agents on data-intensive tasks. Furthermore, UrbanDS has been deployed on the urban operations platform of Dongxihu District, Wuhan, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world urban applications.

AI.tldr: UrbanDS is a graph-guided multi-agent LLM system that organizes urban datasets as reusable skills in a dataset graph and uses specialized agents to plan, execute, and report on data-intensive urban tasks, outperforming existing data science agents and working in real-world deployments.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based data science agents struggle with data-intensive scenarios where relevant information must be discovered and combined from large-scale, heterogeneous datasets. Urban problems are a prime example: urban data are massive, multi-source, and interconnected across space, time, and semantics. There is a need for a system that can automatically organize such datasets, identify their relations, and leverage them effectively for complex urban analysis and modeling tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose UrbanDS, a graph-guided LLM multi-agent system. They first build a unified dataset graph, where each dataset is modeled as a reusable skill node and edges encode inter-dataset relationships. A Data Profiling Agent automatically profiles each dataset and forms its skill representation, while a Relation Agent discovers and encodes relations between datasets. At run time, a Planner Agent queries the dataset graph to select task-relevant datasets and produce an execution plan. Multiple Execution Agents then carry out the actual data processing and analysis, sharing intermediate states via a common memory. Finally, a Report Agent aggregates logs and outputs a report, which can be iteratively refined with user feedback. They also construct UrbanDS-Bench, a benchmark of representative urban data science tasks for systematic evaluation.
AI.result: On both general data science benchmarks and the proposed UrbanDS-Bench urban benchmark, UrbanDS achieves consistently better performance than existing data science LLM agents, especially on data-intensive tasks requiring the combination of multiple heterogeneous datasets. Additionally, the system has been deployed on a real-world urban operations platform in Dongxihu District, Wuhan, showing that the approach is practically effective in operational urban analytics settings.
AI.conclusion: UrbanDS demonstrates that organizing heterogeneous urban datasets into a unified dataset graph of reusable skills, and coordinating specialized LLM agents over this graph, substantially improves performance on data-intensive urban tasks compared to prior data science agents. The introduction of UrbanDS-Bench provides a standardized way to evaluate such systems. The successful real-world deployment indicates that graph-guided multi-agent LLM frameworks are a promising direction for practical urban data science and potentially other domains with large, complex data repositories.

title: Revisiting Lossy Verification in Speculative Decoding: Mechanisms, Trade-offs, and Failure Modes
summary: Speculative Decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by allowing a lightweight draft model to propose tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by a larger target model. Recent approaches introduce lossy verification schemes to further improve efficiency by relaxing strict distributional matching. Yet such relaxation silently rewrites the decoding distribution, and the resulting acceleration can come at the cost of unstable, sometimes severely degraded generation quality. In this work, we present a principled analysis of the distributions induced by lossy verification methods. We show that many seemingly distinct approaches differ only superficially and can be classified into two categories: truncation-based verification and collaborative verification. We further construct a diagnostic evaluation framework across curated benchmarks. For truncation-based methods, we identify a fundamental pitfall: performance can degrade significantly compared to the true truncation sampling baseline due to distributional distortion. For collaborative verification, we uncover a key principles: controlling the overshoot of draft probabilities relative to target probabilities is essential to prevent low-quality outputs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZhouYuxuanYX/Fast-HSD.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why speculative decoding with lossy verification can harm generation quality, classifies existing methods into two main types, and identifies principles to keep them both fast and reliable.
AI.motivation: Speculative Decoding speeds up large language model inference by using a small draft model and a large target model, but newer "lossy" verification tricks, meant to gain even more speed, often degrade output quality in unstable and poorly understood ways. There is a need for a principled, distribution-level understanding of how these lossy methods change the effective decoding distribution and when/why they fail.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze the probability distributions induced by different lossy verification schemes in speculative decoding and show that many prior methods can be unified into two classes: truncation-based verification and collaborative verification. They then build a diagnostic evaluation framework with curated benchmarks that compare these schemes not only on speed but on how their induced distributions and resulting generations deviate from appropriate baselines such as true truncation sampling.
AI.result: They show that truncation-based verification methods can significantly hurt performance relative to the idealized truncation sampling baseline because lossy verification distorts the intended sampling distribution. For collaborative verification methods, they identify that the main determinant of quality is how much the draft model’s probabilities overshoot those of the target model; large overshoots lead to low-quality outputs, while controlling these overshoots preserves quality along with speedups.
AI.conclusion: Lossy verification in speculative decoding cannot be treated as a free efficiency gain: it implicitly alters the decoding distribution and can seriously degrade quality if not carefully designed. Many existing techniques fall into two conceptual families—truncation-based and collaborative verification—and their behavior can be understood through this lens. In particular, truncation-style methods suffer from intrinsic distributional distortion, and collaborative methods must rigorously control draft-model probability overshoot to remain reliable. The provided analysis and diagnostic framework give principled guidance for designing fast yet high-quality speculative decoding algorithms.

title: Do Latent Channels Actually Communicate? A Causal Audit of Latent Multi-Agent LLM
summary: Latent communication in large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) transmits continuous internal representations instead of text, but greater representational capacity does not establish that the receiver uses task-relevant information. End-task performance alone also cannot reveal whether an observed effect depends on message presence, content generated for the evaluated example, or information supplied by a separate agent. We introduce a causal audit that applies controlled message replacements at the boundary where the sender-produced representation enters the receiver. Four message settings support five measurements of encoded sender information, receiver sensitivity to message presence and identity, the task value of example-specific content, and the additional value supplied by a separate agent. We apply the audit to latent relay with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, ARC-C, and MATH-500. On GSM8K, the Qwen3-4B overall performance effect of -1.00 percentage point decomposes into a -6.17-point effect retained by an other-example message and a +5.17-point effect attributable to example-specific content; both component directions reverse at 8B. On MATH-500, the Qwen3-4B gain of 15.00 points comprises 8.33 points retained by an other-example message and 6.67 points attributable to example-specific content, while the 8B gain is dominated by the former component. Self-substitution comparisons further show that example-specific content and other-agent value are distinct. These results show that aggregate accuracy does not identify how a latent message affects the receiver and motivate controlled message comparisons as a standard evaluation for latent communication.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces a causal audit framework to dissect how latent messages in LLM-based multi-agent systems affect downstream performance, showing that overall accuracy hides distinct effects of message presence, example-specific content, and other-agent information.
AI.motivation: In LLM-based multi-agent systems with latent (representation-level) communication, improved end-task performance does not clarify what information in the latent messages is actually used by receivers or how it affects decisions. Existing evaluations cannot disentangle whether performance changes arise from the mere presence of a message, its specific content for a given example, or information injected by additional agents. The authors aim to provide a principled way to causally analyze and quantify what latent messages encode and how they influence receivers, beyond aggregate accuracy metrics.
AI.method: The authors design a causal audit procedure that performs controlled interventions on latent messages at the interface between sender and receiver models. They define four systematically varied message settings, including original messages, ablations, and cross-example or cross-agent substitutions. By swapping or disabling messages while keeping other factors fixed, they obtain five distinct measurements that separately quantify: (1) information encoded by the sender, (2) receiver sensitivity to the presence vs. absence of a message, (3) sensitivity to message identity, (4) task value of example-specific content, and (5) additional value contributed by a separate agent. They implement this on latent relay setups using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across GSM8K, ARC-C, and MATH-500 benchmarks.
AI.result: On GSM8K, for Qwen3-4B, an overall performance change of -1 percentage point due to latent relay decomposes into a -6.17-point effect that persists when replacing the message with one from another example, and a +5.17-point gain attributable specifically to example-dependent content; for Qwen3-8B, both components flip sign, indicating different usage of latent information. On MATH-500, Qwen3-4B’s 15-point gain splits into 8.33 points explainable by information preserved under other-example substitution and 6.67 points from example-specific content, while Qwen3-8B’s improvement is mostly driven by the non-example-specific component. Self-substitution experiments further demonstrate that the benefit from example-specific content is distinct from additional value provided by a separate agent. Across benchmarks, the audit reveals that aggregate accuracy alone does not indicate what aspects of latent communication actually drive receiver behavior.
AI.conclusion: Latent message passing in LLM-based multi-agent systems can influence performance through multiple, separable channels—mere message presence, example-specific content, and extra information from other agents—and aggregate accuracy conceals these underlying mechanisms. The proposed causal audit, based on controlled message replacements at the sender–receiver boundary, provides a structured way to decompose and measure these effects. The findings support using such controlled latent-message comparisons as a standard evaluation protocol for latent communication, enabling more interpretable and reliable analysis of multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Filesystem-Based Memory for LLM Agents: Organization, Evolution, and Sustainability
summary: Deployed LLM agents increasingly keep their long-term memory as a filesystem: a directory tree of markdown files that the agent itself reads, writes, and reorganizes through generic file tools. Yet research has largely passed over this medium: prior systems design bespoke memory representations and study retrieval over them, leaving the default's two working assumptions untested: that an agent can keep a growing store organized as memories accumulate, conflict, and go stale, and that this organization pays. We present the first systematic exploration of filesystem-based memory for LLM agents. We formalize the setting as three roles around one memory filesystem: a management agent integrates and organizes incoming content, a search agent answers queries with cited sources, and an execution agent supplies task trajectories that are distilled into skills, unifying declarative memory and skills in a single store. Across long-conversation benchmarks and embodied tasks, we vary memory shape (agent-organized hierarchy, verbatim dump, chunk retrieval), stream scale, tool harness (sandboxed shell, memory-tool-style functions, varied search tooling), and the strengths of the management and search agents, tracking answer quality, cost, and store health as memory grows. What organization reliably buys is search economy: organized stores roughly halve retrieval cost where material is large. Today's agents, however, fall short of the default's promise: in our growth study, organization erodes for all but the strongest management agent, and no agent we measure converts organization itself into better answers. And the model is not the only lever over a store's shape: changing the tool set alone reshapes the store as strongly as swapping the model. The study turns the filesystem default from an assumption into a design space for agent memory.

AI.tldr: Systematic study of using a markdown-file filesystem as long-term memory for LLM agents, testing whether agent-driven organization helps and under what conditions.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in practice often use simple filesystem-like memory (markdown files in directories), but prior research assumes this works without rigorously testing if agents can maintain organization over time or if organization improves performance and efficiency. There is a need to turn this implicit default into an explicit, evaluated design space.
AI.method: Formalize filesystem memory into three agent roles (management, search, execution) over a shared directory tree. Experiment across long-conversation and embodied-task benchmarks while varying: (1) memory structure (agent-organized hierarchy vs verbatim log vs chunk retrieval), (2) size/scale of the memory stream, (3) tool interface (shell vs memory-function tools vs different search tools), and (4) capability levels of management and search agents. Measure answer quality, retrieval cost, and the health/organization of the memory store as it grows.
AI.result: Organized filesystem memories significantly reduce retrieval cost—about a 2× improvement—when the memory corpus is large. However, most evaluated agents cannot maintain good organization as the memory grows, except for the strongest management model, and even when organization is present it does not translate into better answer quality in the tested settings. Tooling choices (what file/search tools are provided) change the emergent structure of the memory as much as swapping model strengths.
AI.conclusion: Filesystem-based memory should not be treated as a neutral default but as a rich design space. While structured organization can improve search efficiency, current LLM agents are poor long-term curators: organization tends to degrade with scale, and better organization alone does not guarantee better answers. Both model capabilities and tool design critically shape how memory evolves, so future systems should co-design agents, tools, and memory structures rather than assuming a generic filesystem layout suffices.

title: Property-driven Causal Abstractions for Markov Decision Processes
summary: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are widely used as decision-making models, commonly specified over factored state spaces through state variables and their valuations. The exponential blowup in the number of states renders many reasoning tasks in MDPs challenging. Abstractions are promising techniques to reduce MDPs and thus mitigate scalability issues. In this work, we introduce a notion of causality on factored MDPs and a novel property-driven causal abstraction technique that retains many characteristics of the original MDP model. For this, we rely on causal relations over state variable predicates and identify those states that share the same reasons for fulfilling or violating a given abstraction property. We theoretically and empirically compare various causal MDP abstractions using different model types such as MDPs, interval MDPs, or stochastic games. Our evaluation demonstrates the potential of our approach: For several standard benchmarks, we obtain small abstractions that allow us to compute near-optimal policies for the original MDP. Furthermore, our causal abstractions often generalize to related large-scale MDP models.

AI.tldr: They define a new, property-driven causal abstraction for factored MDPs that clusters states sharing the same causal reasons for satisfying/violating a property, yielding smaller models that still admit near-optimal policies and often generalize to larger related MDPs.
AI.motivation: Factored MDPs suffer from exponential state-space explosion, making planning and verification difficult. Existing abstractions may lose important behavioral characteristics of the original model or be insufficiently guided by the properties of interest. The authors aim to develop an abstraction that both scales better and preserves the causal structure relevant to the properties and policies being analyzed.
AI.method: They introduce a formal notion of causality for factored MDPs based on causal relations between state-variable predicates and property satisfaction/violation. Using this, they construct a property-driven causal abstraction: states are grouped if they share the same causal reasons for fulfilling or violating the target property. They instantiate and study these abstractions across different model types, including standard MDPs, interval MDPs, and stochastic games, and compare multiple causal abstraction variants both theoretically and empirically.
AI.result: On several standard benchmark problems, their causal abstraction yields significantly smaller abstract models while still enabling computation of policies that are near-optimal for the original MDP. The experiments also indicate that the constructed causal abstractions are robust enough to transfer or generalize to related, larger-scale MDP models.
AI.conclusion: Causality-based, property-driven abstractions for factored MDPs can effectively mitigate state-space explosion while preserving key behavioral properties relevant for decision making. The proposed approach produces compact abstractions that support near-optimal policy synthesis and often remain useful when applied to related larger models, suggesting a promising direction for scalable analysis and control of complex MDPs.

title: Contrastive ESA: Human Evaluation of Multiple Translations at Once
summary: Current human evaluation of machine translation typically assesses single outputs in isolation, a paradigm that suffers from high annotator noise and cost. We introduce Contrastive Error Span Annotation (cESA), a protocol that presents multiple translations of the source input (text, video, audio, image). In cESA, the annotator sees multiple translations of the same document, marks major and minor error spans, and then assigns a score from 0% to 100% on absolute scale. By allowing annotators to access the shared context across multiple outputs, cESA facilitates more consistent and efficient judgments. We validate cESA using a large-scale human evaluation of English->Japanese translations of 12 models, demonstrating reductions in annotation time and noise compared to standard pointwise evaluation. Unlike existing contrastive ranking methods, cESA yields absolute quality judgments that enable simple, interpretable non-parametric model rankings without the need for post-hoc corrections.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Contrastive Error Span Annotation (cESA), a new human evaluation protocol for machine translation that shows multiple translations at once, has annotators mark error spans and assign absolute quality scores, leading to faster, less noisy, and more interpretable evaluation and model ranking than standard single-output or purely ranking-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing human evaluation of machine translation usually judges one translation at a time (pointwise evaluation). This suffers from high annotator noise, high cost, and inconsistent judgments, partly because annotators lack direct comparison and broader context. Contrastive/ranking methods help but mainly provide relative rankings and often need complex post-hoc corrections to derive system scores. The authors want an evaluation method that is more efficient, yields more consistent judgments, and still produces absolute, interpretable quality scores for each system.
AI.method: They introduce Contrastive Error Span Annotation (cESA). In this protocol, annotators are shown multiple translations of the same source document (which can be text, video, audio, or image-based content). For each translation, annotators mark spans corresponding to major and minor errors, then assign an overall quality score on a 0–100% absolute scale. The shared view over multiple outputs leverages contrastive context while preserving absolute scoring. The authors validate cESA via a large-scale human evaluation of 12 English→Japanese MT models, comparing annotation time, noise, and resulting rankings to those from standard pointwise evaluation and contrastive ranking approaches.
AI.result: In the English→Japanese evaluation with 12 MT models, cESA reduced annotation time and annotator noise compared to standard pointwise evaluation. It produced more consistent judgments and allowed non-parametric ranking of models using the absolute scores, without needing complex post-hoc calibration. The method also retained the advantages of contrastive setups (better use of shared context) while improving interpretability over purely ranking-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: cESA is an effective human evaluation protocol for machine translation that combines contrastive presentation of multiple system outputs with span-based error marking and absolute scoring. It yields faster, more reliable, and more interpretable evaluations than traditional pointwise methods, and unlike other contrastive approaches, it directly provides absolute quality scores that enable straightforward, transparent system ranking without post-processing.

title: From Passive Video to Editable Experience: Physically Grounded Experience Synthesis for Embodied Intelligence
summary: The key bottleneck in embodied AI is not model architecture but data. Although billions of human manipulation videos exist online, robots cannot directly learn from them due to the embodiment gap between human morphology and robot hardware. We introduce Pegasus, a low-resource framework that bridges this gap by translating human demonstrations into robot-learnable data through structured knowledge transfer. Instead of relying on raw video prompts, Pegasus constructs a graph-based intermediate representation: a Task Graph extracted from human videos is transformed through Affordance and Constraint Graphs into a Robot Planning Graph for robot-conditioned video generation. A hierarchical affordance latent space models the relationship between object states, affordances, and tasks, enabling generalization beyond object identities. A closed-loop physics verifier further filters invalid generations using kinematic feasibility, collision constraints, and joint limits. We evaluate Pegasus across a range of egocentric manipulation benchmarks, including GTEA Gaze+ and EPIC-KITCHENS-100, and diverse robot embodiments, assessing Task Correctness, Executability, State Consistency, and Learnability. Results demonstrate reliable cross-embodiment translation and show that robot data generation can be reframed from a hardware collection problem into a scalable, low-resource knowledge transfer problem.

AI.tldr: Pegasus is a framework that converts human manipulation videos into robot-executable data via graph-based task representations, affordance modeling, and physics verification, enabling scalable cross-embodiment learning.
AI.motivation: Embodied AI for robots is bottlenecked by the lack of suitable training data, not model architectures. Although there are billions of human manipulation videos, robots cannot directly learn from them because of the embodiment gap between human bodies and diverse robot hardware. The paper aims to systematically bridge this gap so robots can leverage abundant human video data for learning manipulation skills.
AI.method: The authors propose Pegasus, a low-resource knowledge transfer framework. It first extracts a Task Graph from human demonstration videos. This is then transformed using Affordance and Constraint Graphs into a Robot Planning Graph tailored to a specific robot embodiment. Pegasus uses a hierarchical affordance latent space to capture relations among object states, affordances, and tasks, allowing generalization across different objects. It generates robot-conditioned videos from this planning graph and employs a closed-loop physics verifier that filters out invalid samples based on kinematic feasibility, collision constraints, and joint limits.
AI.result: Pegasus is evaluated on egocentric manipulation benchmarks such as GTEA Gaze+ and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 across multiple robot embodiments. Using metrics including Task Correctness, Executability, State Consistency, and Learnability, the framework shows reliable translation of human demonstrations into robot-usable data and effective cross-embodiment generalization.
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that the main challenge in robot learning from demonstration is data, not architecture, and that human videos can be turned into effective robot training data via structured, graph-based knowledge transfer and verification. Pegasus reframes robot data generation as a scalable, low-resource knowledge transfer problem instead of a costly hardware data collection process, enabling broader and more flexible use of existing human video datasets for embodied AI.

title: Constitutional Midtraining: Content Presence Drives Alignment Gains
summary: Post-training alignment is often shallow, eroding under fine-tuning. Whether midtraining interventions, cleanly isolated from post-training, can produce durable alignment remains untested. We test this via constitutional midtraining: inserting principled, values-based content into midtraining against a replay-only control at 120B scale. Our 394M-token constitutional corpus, built from Anthropic's Constitution, uses a 2x2 factorial design (curriculum ordering x deliberative reasoning) to produce four constitutionally midtrained conditions plus a control, evaluated on self-generated and established benchmarks including alignment under pressure, value conflict resolution, blackmail, and emergent misalignment across three stages: post-midtraining, post-SFT, and post-benign fine-tuning. Constitutionally midtrained models outperform the control on alignment generalization and durability, notably on blackmail: SFT instills a blackmail propensity in all models, but constitutional midtraining blunts it, with the advantage surviving benign fine-tuning (-17.5pp). This durability does not extend to settings requiring active resistance to in-context pressure or conflict, where the advantage attenuates after SFT. The presence of constitutional content at midtraining also matters more than its structure, and constitutional midtraining incurs no cost, on average, on the capabilities we test (MMLU, ARC-Easy, piqa, GSM8K) at any stage. A modest amount of constitutional content at midtraining could therefore yield broad, persistent alignment gains, offering a cheap, complementary addition to SFT-centered pipelines. Code, data, and models are available.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether inserting values-based “constitutional” data during midtraining—rather than only applying post-training alignment—can create more durable alignment in large language models without hurting capabilities.
AI.motivation: Post-training alignment methods like supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RLHF can be shallow: they are easily eroded by later fine-tuning or fail under adversarial pressure. It is unclear whether modifying the base model earlier, during midtraining and in a way cleanly separated from post-training, can yield more deeply internalized and persistent alignment. The authors want to empirically test whether a small amount of well-designed, values-based data, injected at midtraining, can improve alignment robustness and generalization at scale, and how this compares to a pure replay control.
AI.method: The authors build a 394M-token “constitutional” midtraining corpus grounded in Anthropic's Constitution, encoding high-level normative principles. They perform constitutional midtraining at 120B model scale, using a 2x2 factorial design: (1) curriculum ordering (how the constitutional material is presented over training) and (2) presence vs absence of explicit deliberative reasoning. This yields four midtraining conditions plus a replay-only control that matches data size without constitutional content. They then apply standard post-training pipelines (SFT and benign fine-tuning) and evaluate models at three stages—post-midtraining, post-SFT, and post-benign fine-tuning. Evaluation covers both self-generated and established alignment benchmarks, including: alignment under pressure, resolving value conflicts, vulnerability to blackmail behaviors, and emergent misalignment. They also test capabilities using MMLU, ARC-Easy, PIQA, and GSM8K to assess for trade-offs.
AI.result: Constitutionally midtrained models consistently outperform the replay control on measures of alignment generalization and persistence across training stages. In particular, SFT introduces a tendency toward blackmail-like responses in all models, but the models that underwent constitutional midtraining exhibit a significantly reduced blackmail propensity, and this advantage remains even after benign fine-tuning (a reduction of about 17.5 percentage points relative to control). However, in tasks that require the model to actively resist in-context pressure or resolve value conflicts in challenging setups, the alignment advantage from constitutional midtraining diminishes after SFT. Among the constitutional midtraining variants, the mere presence of constitutional content is more important than its specific structure (e.g., curriculum details or explicit deliberation). Across all tested stages, constitutional midtraining does not measurably harm standard capability benchmarks on average.
AI.conclusion: Injecting a relatively small amount of well-chosen, principle-driven constitutional data during midtraining can yield broad and durable alignment gains without sacrificing measured capabilities. These gains are especially notable for reducing harmful behaviors like blackmail and remain robust through subsequent benign fine-tuning, though they are less durable in scenarios requiring strong resistance to in-context pressure or conflicts. Because the exact arrangement of the constitutional material is less important than its inclusion, constitutional midtraining appears to be a simple, low-cost and complementary addition to SFT-centric alignment pipelines, potentially improving the depth and robustness of model alignment at scale.

title: What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation
comment: 17 pages (11 main + appendices), 7 figures. Accepted at the North East AI Agents Day 2026 workshop, Jane Street, New York City. Workshop: https://ne-agents-day.github.io/
summary: Bot detectors deployed at scale treat traffic as binary: human or bot. This assumption breaks when AI agents browse the web through browser automation, a traffic class that is neither and that binary classifiers structurally cannot represent. We present a three-class detection framework distinguishing humans, bots, and AI agents, and show that the binary-vs-agent confusion is architectural: a binary human-vs-bot detector misroutes agent sessions because its label space lacks an agent class. On our controlled benchmark, an MLP binary classifier misclassifies 39.1% of real AI agents as human and a SAINT binary transformer misclassifies 34.5%; adding an explicit agent class yields per-class agent F1 = 1.000 in all 30 runs (3 model families $\times$ 10 seeds). To measure evasion resistance, we construct a five-level evasion ladder spanning passive observation, GAN-generated trajectories, and replay of real human cursor data ($n = 2299$ evasion sessions). Across 10 seeds and 3 model families we observe zero agent misses in 22990 per-seed predictions. The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning: Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams a physical input device produces, and this absence signature survives trajectory manipulation. Exhaustive search over all feature subsets of size 1-5 (9401 GBMs) shows that two behavioral features (mouse_event_rate, teleport_click_ratio) give 100% observed agent recall at every evasion level with agent precision 0.994; five features lift macro-F1 to 0.991. The signal is redundantly encoded: removing teleport_click_ratio leaves agent detection at 100%. The single-feature regime is degenerate, flagging every agent only by collapsing the classifier to always predict "agent". Two features robustly isolate agents; five separate all three traffic classes at macro-F1 $\geq 0.99$.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current web bot detectors fail on AI agent traffic and proposes a three-class model (human, bot, AI agent) that can reliably spot AI agents by exploiting browser automation artifacts.
AI.motivation: Web bot detection systems assume all traffic is either human or bot. AI agents using browser automation fall in between and are systematically misclassified because the label space has no separate agent class. The authors want to (1) demonstrate this structural limitation of binary classifiers, and (2) design a practical, robust way to detect AI agents even when they try to evade detection.
AI.method: They build a three-class detection framework (human, traditional bot, AI agent) and evaluate multiple model families (including MLP and SAINT transformer) on a controlled benchmark. They compare binary vs three-class setups, then construct a five-level “evasion ladder” for AI agents: from simple passive observation to advanced evasions like GAN-generated mouse trajectories and replay of real human cursor data. They train thousands of gradient-boosted models over all feature subsets of size 1–5 to isolate which behavioral features are sufficient for robust agent detection.
AI.result: Binary human-vs-bot models misroute a large fraction of AI agent traffic: an MLP misclassifies 39.1% of AI agents as human, and a SAINT transformer misclassifies 34.5%. When an explicit agent class is added, agent F1 reaches 1.000 for all runs across 3 model families and 10 seeds. Under 2299 evasion sessions per seed (22990 total per-seed predictions across 10 seeds and 3 families), they observe zero missed AI agents. Two simple behavioral features—mouse_event_rate and teleport_click_ratio—are enough to achieve 100% observed agent recall at all evasion levels, with agent precision 0.994; using five features raises macro-F1 to 0.991. The discriminative signal stems from Playwright’s automation artifact: it doesn’t emit the raw continuous pointer and wheel delta streams that human input devices do, and this absence signature persists under trajectory manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Binary bot detectors are structurally incapable of correctly routing AI agent traffic because they lack an agent label; introducing a third “agent” class fixes this and yields highly reliable detection in their setting. The core signal is not cognitive behavior but low-level browser automation artifacts, especially missing fine-grained input events, which remain detectable even under sophisticated evasion attempts. Only a handful of behavioral features are required to reliably distinguish humans, bots, and AI agents, achieving macro-F1 ≥ 0.99, implying that robust AI-agent detection is feasible today but heavily dependent on automation stack details like Playwright’s event emission behavior.

title: Automated Multilabel Mpox Research Classification with Explainable Transformer Models
summary: The Mpox outbreak remains a serious public health issue, with the WHO (World Health Organization) reporting increasing cases in some regions. Research on Mpox is vital for several reasons, including vaccine development, diagnostic improvement, viral evolution studies, and preventing future outbreaks. However, the large amount of research being published makes it difficult to organize and analyze information efficiently. This study focuses on using multilabel classification to categorize 14590 Mpox research articles into key topics such as outbreaks, vaccination, and epidemiology. Among the different AI models tested, BERT performed the best, achieving 97.05% accuracy, 97.67% micro F1 score, and 96.46% macro F1 score. To better understand how the model makes decisions, SHAP was used to analyze significant word features and patterns. The results show that BERT can help automate the classification of Mpox research, making it easier for researchers, policymakers, and healthcare workers to quickly find relevant information, saving time and improving public health efforts.

AI.tldr: They build an AI-based multilabel classifier (best: BERT) to automatically categorize Mpox research papers into topical labels, enabling faster literature organization and retrieval.
AI.motivation: Mpox remains a growing public health concern, with rising case numbers and a rapidly expanding, fragmented scientific literature. Researchers, policymakers, and clinicians need to quickly find relevant studies on topics such as outbreaks, vaccination, diagnostics, and epidemiology, but manual screening and organization of thousands of papers is inefficient and error-prone. There is therefore a need for automated methods to structure and classify Mpox research to support timely evidence use and future outbreak preparedness.
AI.method: They collected 14,590 Mpox-related research articles and framed the task as a multilabel text classification problem, where each article can belong to multiple topical categories (e.g., outbreaks, vaccination, epidemiology). They experimented with different AI/NLP models and identified BERT as the best-performing architecture. The BERT model was trained and evaluated on this labeled corpus. To provide model interpretability, they applied SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to identify important word features and patterns that influence the model’s topic predictions, thereby opening the black box of the classifier to some extent.
AI.result: Among all tested models, BERT achieved the highest performance, with 97.05% accuracy, 97.67% micro F1 score, and 96.46% macro F1 score for multilabel topic classification of Mpox papers. The SHAP analysis highlighted which words and textual patterns were most influential in BERT’s decisions, demonstrating that the model’s behavior aligns with domain-relevant cues in the text. These results indicate that the system can reliably and transparently categorize large volumes of Mpox literature into meaningful thematic groups.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that BERT-based multilabel classification is an effective tool for organizing the rapidly growing Mpox research literature. With high predictive performance and interpretable feature attributions via SHAP, the approach can automate topic tagging of thousands of articles, allowing researchers, policymakers, and healthcare workers to more quickly locate pertinent information. This can reduce time spent on manual screening and support more efficient, evidence-informed responses to ongoing and future Mpox public health challenges.

title: Belief-Guided Decision Making with Uncertainty Gating in the Game of Go
summary: Recent advancements in Computer Go, driven by AlphaZero and MuZero, rely heavily on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to correct the errors of the neural network policy. While effective on massive computational clusters, this dependence creates a critical bottleneck on consumer-grade hardware, where the computational cost of tree management severely limits inference rates. Furthermore, without deep search, these models suffer from hallucination, proposing moves with high confidence that are strategically fatal. This paper introduces a novel Belief-Guided architecture that disentangles the Policy head from a distinct Belief head. Unlike traditional value functions, the Belief head acts as an internal simulator and independent critic, modeling epistemic uncertainty and strategic stability. By integrating memory mechanisms (Transformer/GRU) to handle long-term dependencies and the Ko rule, and utilizing a gating mechanism to filter overconfident policy errors, our model shifts the burden of intelligence from runtime search to parametric "intuition." Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves search-free win rates and reduces hallucination, enabling professional-level play on limited hardware where massive MCTS is infeasible.

AI.tldr: Belief-Guided Go AI separates fast move suggestion from an internal belief model that estimates uncertainty and strategic stability, reducing reliance on expensive MCTS while avoiding confident but catastrophic blunders.
AI.motivation: AlphaZero-style Go engines achieve high strength by combining neural policies with heavy MCTS, but this is impractical on consumer hardware because tree search is computationally expensive. When search is shallow or absent, these systems hallucinate: they output overconfident, strategically losing moves. The paper aims to design an architecture that performs strong, search-free play and is robust against such hallucinations, making professional-level Go more accessible without large compute.
AI.method: The authors propose a Belief-Guided architecture with two separate heads: a Policy head that proposes moves and a Belief head acting as an internal simulator/critic. The Belief head models epistemic uncertainty and strategic stability rather than only scalar value, and is implemented with memory mechanisms (Transformer/GRU) to capture long-term dependencies such as Ko. A gating mechanism uses the Belief head’s outputs to detect overconfident or unstable policy suggestions and filter or adjust them, effectively replacing much of MCTS’s corrective role with parametric reasoning learned in the network.
AI.result: Experiments show that the Belief-Guided model attains substantially higher win rates when used without or with minimal MCTS, compared to traditional AlphaZero-style architectures. It also exhibits fewer hallucinated, high-confidence blunders. Overall, the system achieves professional-level or near-professional-level play on limited hardware where massive tree search is not feasible.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling policy from a belief/uncertainty model and using the latter to gate decisions can reduce dependence on heavy search in Go engines. The Belief-Guided architecture shifts strategic reasoning from runtime MCTS into the network parameters, enabling strong, low-search play and mitigating hallucination, which is especially valuable for resource-constrained environments.

title: AtmosERC: Modeling Dialogue-Level Affective Atmosphere for Emotion Recognition in Conversation
summary: Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) aims to predict utterance-level emotions in dialogues and has largely advanced through context-centric modeling. However, global context is a heterogeneous signal, and not all contextual information is equally relevant to emotion prediction. This paper focuses on the affect-oriented component of this signal, termed dialogue-level affective atmosphere, which captures a latent tendency commonly reflected in conversational emotion patterns. To estimate and exploit this tendency, we propose AtmosERC, a graph-based ERC framework that models each dialogue as a conversational graph over utterances and speakers. A relation-aware graph extractor filters and fuses heterogeneous graph signals to produce dialogue-level and speaker-conditioned affective priors. The resulting compact prior guides lightweight sequential emotion prediction and can also be verbalized into prompt-level cues for LLM-based ERC without modifying backbone models. Experiments on four ERC benchmarks show that AtmosERC improves lightweight ERC, enhances LLM-based ERC as a plug-in cue, and yields more stable predictions under local emotional deviations.

AI.tldr: They propose AtmosERC, a graph-based framework that extracts a dialogue-level "affective atmosphere" prior to improve emotion recognition in conversations, both for lightweight models and as cues for LLMs.
AI.motivation: Most ERC methods rely heavily on raw conversational context, but this global context is heterogeneous: some parts are emotionally informative while others are distracting or irrelevant. The authors want to isolate and explicitly model the context component that reflects the overall emotional tendency of a dialogue (the "affective atmosphere") to make predictions more accurate and robust, especially when local utterances deviate from the main emotional flow.
AI.method: They introduce AtmosERC, which represents each dialogue as a graph whose nodes are utterances and speakers, with relations encoding conversational structure. A relation-aware graph extractor processes this graph to filter and combine heterogeneous graph signals into: (1) a dialogue-level affective prior representing the overall emotional atmosphere, and (2) speaker-conditioned affective priors capturing each speaker’s typical emotional tendency in that dialogue. These compact priors then guide a lightweight sequential emotion classifier. In addition, the priors can be verbalized as natural-language cues (prompts) to steer large language models for ERC without changing their parameters.
AI.result: On four standard ERC benchmarks, AtmosERC leads to higher performance than baseline lightweight ERC models, improves the ERC behavior of LLMs when used as an additional prompt cue, and produces more stable and consistent emotion predictions in cases where individual utterances temporarily diverge from the dialogue’s main emotional tendency.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly estimating a dialogue-level affective atmosphere via relation-aware graph modeling yields useful affective priors. These priors improve both conventional lightweight ERC models and LLM-based ERC without finetuning, and they make emotion predictions more robust to local emotional fluctuations within conversations.

title: Setoka: A Benchmark for Hierarchical User Understanding in Personalized Agents over Heterogeneous Data
summary: Personalized agents are increasingly applied to assist users across a wide range of tasks. Effective personalized assistance requires not only retrieving explicit facts from past interactions stored in agent memory, but also inferring abstract personal characteristics. However, existing memory benchmarks primarily evaluate whether an agent can retrieve information explicitly stated in conversational histories, failing to provide an effective assessment of deeper user understanding. In this work, we propose Setoka, a benchmark for evaluating memory-augmented personalized agents with hierarchical user understanding from heterogeneous data. Grounded in theories from cognitive and personality psychology, Setoka defines four levels of user understanding, i.e., semantic memory, episodic memory, behavior pattern, and personality trait. Moreover, to enable realistic yet privacy-preserving evaluation, we design a psychometrics-based pipeline that synthesizes diverse, coherent heterogeneous user data and queries at scale. Finally, we leverage Setoka to evaluate 3 language models combined with 5 memory systems for 10 synthetic users. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that while existing systems perform well on semantic memory retrieval, their performance declines on episodic memory. Moreover, when dealing with behavior pattern and personality trait understanding tasks that require integrating heterogeneous and fragmented information dispersed over time, performance declines even further. These findings demonstrate that user understanding cannot be handled by simple fact retrieval, motivating the design of memory mechanisms for cross-source integration and abstraction over long-term user behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Setoka, a new benchmark to evaluate how well memory-augmented personalized agents understand users beyond simple fact retrieval, across four levels of user understanding from multiple heterogeneous data sources.
AI.motivation: Current personalized agents and their memory benchmarks focus mainly on retrieving explicitly stated facts from user-agent interaction histories. This misses deeper aspects of user understanding, such as inferring patterns of behavior or stable personality traits from fragmented and heterogeneous data. The authors are motivated to fill this evaluation gap so that future systems can be designed and measured against richer notions of user understanding grounded in cognitive and personality psychology.
AI.method: The authors design Setoka, a benchmark grounded in psychological theories that formalizes four hierarchical levels of user understanding: (1) semantic memory (factual user info), (2) episodic memory (event-specific info), (3) behavior patterns (regularities over time and contexts), and (4) personality traits (stable dispositions). They build a psychometrics-inspired data synthesis pipeline to generate realistic but privacy-preserving heterogeneous user data and corresponding queries at scale. They then test 3 different language models combined with 5 distinct memory systems on 10 synthetic users using the Setoka tasks.
AI.result: Across the evaluation, systems generally perform well on tasks requiring retrieval of semantic memory. Performance drops noticeably on episodic memory tasks and declines even more for behavior pattern and personality trait tasks, which require integrating fragmented, heterogeneous information over time. This shows a consistent difficulty gradient as the level of abstraction and required integration increases.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that simple fact-retrieval mechanisms are insufficient for true user understanding in personalized agents. As the task moves from semantic and episodic memory toward behavior patterns and personality traits, existing memory systems degrade sharply. This highlights the need for new memory architectures and mechanisms that can integrate information across sources and time and support abstraction over long-term user behavior, and positions Setoka as a benchmark to drive and evaluate such advances.

title: Phoneme- vs. Character-Level Targets and Selective State-Space Models for Intracortical Brain-to-Text
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables, submitted to IberSPEECH 2026
summary: State-of-the-art intracortical brain-to-text systems pair a neural-sequence phone decoder with an external language model. Two design axes remain underexplored: whether selective state-space models (Mamba) improve on recurrent decoders, and how the output target (phonetic vs.\ character) interacts with that choice. On the public Brain-to-Text '25 benchmark, we study a controlled 2x2 grid (GRU vs.\ hybrid Mamba decoder; phonetic vs.\ character targets) trained with a CTC objective under one reproducible protocol. The recurrent baseline remains strongest: the best phonetic GRU reaches 12.62\% PER and 21.19\% WER, while the best textual GRU after LM rescoring reaches 13.39\% CER and 26.28\% WER. The Mamba hybrid is competitive but does not surpass it. Ablations isolate architectural contributions, and error analysis shows representation-dependent failures: articulatory-like phoneme confusions vs.\ lexical and word-boundary errors.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares GRU-based and Mamba-hybrid neural decoders, and phonetic vs. character output targets, for intracortical brain-to-text decoding on the Brain-to-Text '25 benchmark, finding that GRU baselines still perform best and that different targets lead to distinct error profiles.
AI.motivation: Intracortical brain-to-text systems currently rely on neural phone decoders plus external language models, but it is unclear whether newer selective state-space models like Mamba can outperform established recurrent decoders, and how the choice of output representation (phonemes vs characters) affects performance and error types under a unified, reproducible setup.
AI.method: The authors define a controlled 2x2 experimental grid on the Brain-to-Text '25 benchmark: GRU vs. hybrid Mamba decoders and phonetic vs. character targets, all trained with a CTC objective under a single, reproducible training protocol. They evaluate performance in terms of phoneme error rate (PER), character error rate (CER), and word error rate (WER), perform ablations to disentangle architectural contributions, and conduct error analysis to categorize failure modes by representation type.
AI.result: The recurrent GRU baseline remains best overall. The top phonetic GRU model achieves 12.62% phoneme error rate and 21.19% word error rate. The best character-based GRU, after language-model rescoring, attains 13.39% character error rate and 26.28% word error rate. Hybrid Mamba decoders are competitive with but do not surpass GRU performance. Ablation studies and detailed error analysis reveal that phonetic models tend to make articulatory-like phoneme confusions, while character models suffer more from lexical and word-boundary errors.
AI.conclusion: Despite the promise of selective state-space models such as Mamba, traditional GRU recurrent decoders still provide superior performance for intracortical brain-to-text decoding on the evaluated benchmark. The choice of output target (phonetic vs character) not only affects accuracy but also qualitatively changes error patterns, indicating that representation selection should be informed by the desired trade-off between articulatory-level and lexical-level robustness.

title: On-Policy Distillation for LLM Safety: A Routing Approach to Template-Robust Realignment
summary: Fine-tuning is the dominant paradigm for specializing large language models (LLMs), yet it exposes a critical vulnerability: malicious data providers can embed harmful behaviors into downstream corpora, creating models that retain professional skills while violating human values on demand. Existing safety-realignment defenses often fail in practice due to three key limitations: they frequently cause catastrophic forgetting of specialized skills; their effectiveness collapses when the defender cannot observe the attacker's prompt template; and successfully realigned models remain susceptible to re-jailbreaking via simple system prompt switches. To address these challenges, we propose Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), a novel realignment framework that models the divergence between aligned and compromised output probability distributions rather than fitting specific prompt templates. We conduct extensive experiments comparing ROPD against four state-of-the-art baselines across three datasets and three base models with varying alignment strengths. Our results demonstrate that when baseline defenses face template mismatches, often accompanied by severe degradation in downstream task performance. In contrast, ROPD substantially mitigates template-mismatch risks, maintaining superior robustness in both defense effectiveness and capability preservation. While our analysis indicates ROPD is not entirely immune to template shifts, its performance degradation is negligible compared to existing methods, establishing a new standard for robust LLM realignment.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies vulnerabilities in fine-tuning large language models and proposes a new defense method, Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), which realigns compromised models more robustly across different prompt templates while preserving their specialized capabilities.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning is commonly used to specialize LLMs, but malicious data providers can poison fine-tuning data so that models appear aligned yet exhibit harmful behavior under specific prompts. Existing realignment defenses often lead to catastrophic forgetting of specialized skills, fail when the defender does not know the attacker’s exact prompt template, and can be bypassed by simple system prompt changes. There is a need for a robust realignment method that preserves capabilities and remains effective under prompt/template shifts.
AI.method: The authors introduce Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), a framework that learns from the difference between the output probability distributions of an aligned model and a compromised (backdoored) model. Instead of defending against specific attack prompts, ROPD models distributional divergence and uses routing plus distillation on-policy (using the defended model’s own rollouts) to guide the compromised model back toward aligned behavior while preserving its specialized skills.
AI.result: Across three datasets and three LLM bases with different alignment strengths, ROPD is compared to four state-of-the-art realignment defenses. When there are prompt template mismatches between attack and defense, baselines often suffer large drops in both safety and task performance, whereas ROPD retains high task performance and strong defense effectiveness. ROPD shows substantially reduced vulnerability to template mismatch, with only minor performance degradation.
AI.conclusion: ROPD provides a more robust approach to LLM realignment than existing methods, especially under mismatched or shifting prompt templates. It better preserves the model’s downstream capabilities while mitigating harmful backdoored behaviors. Although it is not completely immune to template shifts, its performance drop is small relative to prior work, setting a new robustness benchmark for safety realignment of fine-tuned LLMs.

title: Metis: Memory Foundation Model
summary: Recent advances in AI agents have increasingly internalized native capabilities into their underlying foundation models, giving rise to multimodal foundation models and large reasoning models. However, agent memory is still primarily implemented through external modules, leaving the native memory capability largely unexplored. In this paper, we take a first step toward this direction by introducing memory foundation models, which empower foundation models with native memory capabilities. We formalize native memory from two perspectives: a persistent and dynamically evolving memory state within the backbone, and native memory procedures that autonomously store and utilize information through model computation. We show that native memory offers advantages in architecture, end-to-end optimization, and efficiency. Based on this formulation, we propose Metis, the first prototype of memory foundation models. Metis introduces a new architecture that equips a foundation model with a native memory state, allowing historical information to be compressed into the model and accessed through memory attention. We construct large-scale memory-specific training data and introduce multiple optimization objectives to acquire these native memory procedures through mid-training. The online memory maintenance of Metis is gradient-free, and the memory update requires only a forward pass. At inference time, all learned model weights remain frozen, while the native memory states are autonomously transformed through standard forward computation. Through extensive experiments, we show that Metis exhibits native memory capabilities and further provide a detailed analysis of its strengths, limitations, and behaviors. To facilitate future research on memory foundation models, we release our project and model checkpoints.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes memory foundation models, introducing native memory directly into foundation models via a prototype called Metis, which maintains and updates a persistent memory state through standard forward passes, improving efficiency and end-to-end optimization for agent memory.
AI.motivation: While recent AI agents have integrated many capabilities natively into large foundation models (e.g., multimodal understanding and reasoning), memory is still largely handled by external modules or tool-like components. This separation limits architectural elegance, end-to-end trainability, efficiency, and potentially capability. The authors are motivated to explore whether memory can be made a first-class, native component of the model itself, allowing agents to maintain and evolve internal memory states without extra systems.
AI.method: The authors formalize "native memory" from two angles: (1) a persistent, dynamically evolving memory state inside the backbone model, and (2) memory procedures—learned behaviors for storing and using information—realized through normal model computation. They instantiate this via Metis, a new architecture that augments a foundation model with an internal memory state accessed via memory attention. They build large-scale, memory-focused training data and define multiple mid-training objectives to teach the model how to manage this memory. Memory maintenance during online use is gradient-free: memory updates only require forward passes, and at inference, model parameters are frozen while the memory state evolves autonomously.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that Metis can indeed maintain and exploit a native memory state over time, showing emergent memory capabilities consistent with the authors' formulation. The model can compress historical information into its memory state and retrieve it through attention, doing so efficiently without backpropagation at inference. The paper reports quantitative and qualitative evaluations and ablations that characterize Metis’s strengths and limitations as a memory foundation model.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that native memory can be successfully integrated into foundation models, yielding architectural and efficiency benefits and enabling new memory behaviors in AI agents. Metis serves as a first prototype of "memory foundation models," validating the feasibility of persistent internal memory states and learned memory procedures. The authors release code and checkpoints to encourage further work on this new class of models and to explore improvements over the current limitations they identify.

title: AgentMap: Joint Equivalence and Subsumption Discovery for Ontology Matching
summary: Ontology matching (OM) has traditionally been formulated as either equivalence discovery or subsumption matching. The existing OM systems identify only one type of semantic correspondence and cannot simultaneously discover equivalence and subsumption mappings. In this paper, we introduce Hybrid Ontology Matching (HOM), a new OM task that unifies equivalence and subsumption discovery, and accordingly propose a Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent OM framework AgentMap that is implemented by a series of interdependent semantic decisions. Given a concept in the source ontology, AgentMap integrates semantic retrieval, hierarchical search, and collaborative multi-agent LLM reasoning to progressively explore the target ontology, identifying either the equivalent concept, if one exists, or the most fine-grained subsumer. We further extend four OM datasets for a HOM benchmark and evaluate AgentMap under hybrid, equivalence-only, and subsumption-only settings. Experimental results show that AgentMap achieves promising performance on the hybrid setting, and at the same time outperforms equivalence matching and subsumption matching baselines on the equivalence-only and subsumption-only settings, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Hybrid Ontology Matching (HOM) and a multi-agent LLM framework, AgentMap, that can jointly discover equivalence and subsumption relations between ontologies, outperforming prior systems on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing ontology matching systems typically handle only one semantic relation type at a time—either equivalence or subsumption—so they cannot jointly discover both types of correspondences in a unified process. This limits their applicability in complex knowledge integration scenarios where concepts across ontologies may be related in multiple ways, not just strict equivalence. The authors are motivated to define and address a more realistic and expressive matching task that integrates these relation types and to leverage recent advances in LLMs to perform richer semantic reasoning over ontology structures.
AI.method: The authors define a new task called Hybrid Ontology Matching (HOM), which unifies equivalence and subsumption discovery in a single framework. They propose AgentMap, an LLM-based multi-agent ontology matching framework that decomposes matching into a sequence of interdependent semantic decisions.
