For each source ontology concept, AgentMap: (1) performs semantic retrieval over the target ontology; (2) explores the target ontology hierarchy via hierarchical search; and (3) uses collaborative reasoning among multiple LLM-based agents to determine whether there is an equivalent concept or, if not, to identify the most fine-grained subsuming target concept. They also construct a HOM benchmark by extending four existing ontology matching datasets and evaluate AgentMap under three settings: hybrid, equivalence-only, and subsumption-only.
AI.result: On the new HOM benchmark, AgentMap demonstrates strong performance on the hybrid setting, successfully identifying both equivalence and subsumption correspondences. In addition, when evaluated in restricted equivalence-only and subsumption-only configurations, AgentMap outperforms specialized baselines designed for equivalence matching and subsumption matching, respectively. This indicates that the hybrid multi-agent LLM approach is competitive or superior even when reduced to traditional single-relation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that ontology matching can be more effectively addressed by a unified hybrid formulation that simultaneously discovers equivalence and subsumption relations. The proposed AgentMap framework, based on multi-agent LLM reasoning combined with semantic retrieval and hierarchical search, provides a practical solution to this Hybrid Ontology Matching task. Its strong empirical results across hybrid and single-relation settings suggest that LLM-based multi-agent architectures are a promising direction for more expressive and accurate ontology alignment in knowledge integration applications.

title: Relation Geometry in Semantic Space of Language Models
summary: When it comes to generating vector representations of words, current language models are achieving high-quality results. However, what is not known is the extent to which knowledge about semantic relations is represented in the geometry of the semantic spaces created in this way. In order to answer this question, we study the relation geometry of such semantic spaces from three perspectives. We first examine whether words standing in a particular relation to a target word~(called relata) occupy the same region in semantic space, and whether the regions corresponding to different relations are distinct from each other. We then verify to what extent semantic spaces reflect certain well-known properties of relations, such as symmetry, asymmetry, and transitivity. Finally, we consider which information about the target words and relata is more important for relation geometry: their surface forms, or their contexts. We conduct experiments on six semantic relations using causal, masked, and diffusion language models. The results show that relata in asymmetric relations relatively clearly occupy a distinct region in semantic space. Asymmetric relations' properties are only moderately well encoded in the semantic space, yet better than those of symmetric ones. Furthermore, when considering the question which information source has the strongest impact on results amongst the models we evaluated, we find that lexical information tends to be more important for the causal language model, whereas contextual information is more important for the masked and diffusion language models. Our results empirically show that relation geometry is not equally well-represented for all relations in semantic space, suggesting that there is a difference in how well semantic relations might be learned from distributional information alone.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how well different types of semantic relations are encoded in the geometry of word embedding spaces produced by modern language models.
AI.motivation: Although modern language models produce high‑quality word vectors, it is unclear how explicitly and systematically semantic relations between words (e.g., causal, asymmetric, symmetric relations) are captured in the geometry of these vector spaces. Understanding this helps clarify what kind of relational knowledge can be learned from distributional data and how different model architectures encode such knowledge.
AI.method: The authors analyze the “relation geometry” of semantic spaces learned by causal, masked, and diffusion language models on six types of semantic relations. (1) They test whether words that stand in a particular relation to a target word (relata) cluster in the same region of the space and whether different relations form distinct regions. (2) They check whether the geometry of these spaces reflects logical/structural properties of relations such as symmetry, asymmetry, and transitivity. (3) They compare the relative importance of lexical (surface-form) information versus contextual information for shaping relation geometry, across model types.
AI.result: They find that for asymmetric relations, relata tend to form relatively clear, distinct regions in the embedding space, more so than for symmetric relations. The formal properties of asymmetric relations (e.g., directionality) are only moderately encoded, but still better than the properties of symmetric relations. Across model architectures, causal language models rely more on lexical (surface-form) information for encoding relation geometry, while masked and diffusion models rely more on contextual information.
AI.conclusion: Relation geometry is unevenly represented across different semantic relations in word embedding spaces. Asymmetric relations are captured more clearly than symmetric ones, and there are systematic differences between model architectures in whether lexical or contextual information dominates. This suggests that not all semantic relations can be learned equally well from distributional information alone and that model design and training objectives influence how relational knowledge is embedded in semantic space.

title: Linguistic Monoculture in LLM-Assisted Language Use
summary: Writing and communication are increasingly mediated by large language models (LLMs) that are being used to draft, revise and polish text. Although such assistance can improve clarity and help authors meet institutional expectations, widespread reliance on shared models may reduce population-level variation in linguistic form, a phenomenon we refer to as linguistic monoculture. We develop a mathematical framework in which authors and LLMs are represented as distributions over linguistic features and coevolve through repeated interaction. We analyze three interaction mechanisms: a shared model with a fixed linguistic distribution, a shared model recursively updated from author outputs, and personalized models updated through author-specific and population-level feedback. We characterize the resulting equilibria and convergence rates, showing that, shared models can drive authors toward a common norm, recursive feedback relocates the shared norm without altering pairwise spread under common conformity, and personalization can preserve a family of distinct author-model equilibria with nonzero linguistic diversity. We then endogenize conformity as a strategic choice trading off private benefits from clarity, legibility, and perceived fluency against distinctive style. Within this utility model, individually rational authors may conform more than is socially optimal because they do not internalize the value their distinctiveness provides to others, creating a negative externality and a price of monoculture that is finite for each fixed instance but can grow without bound when distinctiveness dominates authenticity. Synthetic simulations illustrate how fixed shared assistance, recursive feedback, and personalization produce different long-run diversity outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper models how widespread use of shared LLMs can reduce linguistic diversity and explores mechanisms (shared, recursively updated, and personalized models) that influence long-run language variation.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly mediate writing, they may standardize language, reducing variation in style and expression (linguistic monoculture). The paper aims to formally understand how different ways of deploying and updating LLMs affect population-level linguistic diversity and the social tradeoffs between clarity and distinctiveness.
AI.method: The authors build a mathematical framework where both authors and LLMs are represented as probability distributions over linguistic features. They analyze three interaction mechanisms: (1) a fixed shared model that does not update, (2) a shared model that is recursively updated based on author outputs, and (3) personalized models updated using both individual and aggregate feedback. They derive equilibria and convergence rates for each mechanism and embed this in a utility model where authors choose their level of conformity versus distinctiveness. They complement the theory with synthetic simulations to visualize long-run diversity outcomes.
AI.result: For a fixed shared model, authors’ language converges toward a common norm, reducing diversity. Recursive feedback shifts the common norm’s location but, under common conformity preferences, does not change the amount of linguistic spread between authors. Personalized models can sustain multiple distinct author–model equilibria, maintaining nonzero linguistic diversity. In the strategic choice framework, individually rational authors over-conform relative to the social optimum because they neglect the positive externality their distinctiveness provides to others, yielding a measurable “price of monoculture.” This price is bounded for fixed parameters but can grow without bound when distinctiveness becomes much more valuable than authenticity.
AI.conclusion: LLM-mediated writing can systematically push populations toward linguistic monoculture depending on how the models are shared and updated. Fixed and shared models promote convergence to a common norm, while personalization can preserve diversity. When authors strategically balance clarity against style, decentralized choices lead to excessive conformity and a negative externality on linguistic diversity. The design of LLM assistance—especially the choice between shared versus personalized models and how feedback is aggregated—plays a critical role in preserving or eroding linguistic variation.

title: Enhancing Generative Information Extraction with Two-step Validation: A Product Attribute Use Case
summary: The ability of large language models (LLMs) to process and generate text has introduced potential for applications in information extraction (IE). While it's debated whether LLMs outperform smaller fine-tuned models for classification tasks, their strong generalization capability makes them promising for domains with limited labeled data available for fine-tuning. This advantage is particularly relevant for the emerging application of the digital product passport (DPP), where the problem space is broad but domain-specific data remains scarce. Motivated by this use case, we apply generative IE to the product domain, explicitly addressing efficiency, generalizability, and data privacy constraints. We propose a two-step validation method that integrates a PLM block into the generative IE pipeline and thereby leverages LLMs' correction capability. We discover that such a validation task enhances LLM performance, particularly on the extraction of weakly expressed, low-salience entities that appear sparsely throughout the text. For certain entities, the performance of mid-size models can even reach levels comparable to larger models, and the improvement of first-step PLM predictions also enhance the final LLM output. Nevertheless, the effects on the smallest open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.2 3B) is limited. Based on the findings, we develop a demo application for product information extraction that utilizes locally deployed LLMs, targeting further adaptations to real-world DPP use cases.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using large language models for generative information extraction in the product domain, proposing a two-step validation pipeline that improves extraction of hard-to-detect entities and enables effective use of mid-size, locally deployed models for digital product passport applications.
AI.motivation: Digital Product Passports require extracting a broad range of product information from text, but labeled data is scarce and the problem space is large. While LLMs generalize well, it's unclear how to best exploit them for information extraction under constraints of efficiency, generalizability, and data privacy, especially when relying on locally deployable models rather than very large proprietary systems.
AI.method: The authors design a generative information extraction pipeline tailored to product-related texts and DPP needs. They introduce a two-step validation method in which a pretrained language model (PLM) block is inserted into the pipeline: first, a PLM generates initial predictions, and then an LLM performs a validation/correction step over these outputs, leveraging its generative and corrective abilities. They systematically compare different model sizes (including small, mid-size, and large LLMs such as Llama-3.2 3B) and analyze performance on entities of varying salience and frequency.
AI.result: The two-step PLM+LLM validation approach enhances extraction performance, particularly for weakly expressed, low-salience entities that appear sparsely in the text. Mid-size LLMs, when combined with this validation step, can reach performance levels close to larger models on certain entity types. Improvements in the first-step PLM predictions propagate to better final LLM outputs. However, the smallest open-source LLMs, such as Llama-3.2 3B, benefit only marginally from this method.
AI.conclusion: A validation-oriented generative IE pipeline that couples a PLM with an LLM is effective for product information extraction under DPP-like constraints, improving the detection of difficult entities and enabling mid-size, locally deployable models to approach the performance of larger LLMs. Nonetheless, there are limits to how much very small open-source models can be boosted. The authors encapsulate their findings in a demo system that shows the feasibility of privacy-preserving, local LLM-based IE for real-world Digital Product Passport scenarios.

title: OmegaUse-OfficeVal: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Office-Suite Tasks with Economic Grounding
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to assist users in completing tasks. However, existing benchmarks provide limited support for evaluating whether agents can carry out office-suite workflows at a reasonable cost. We introduce OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on long-horizon office-suite tasks with task-level economic grounding. The benchmark comprises 100 tasks derived from office-suite requests proposed by practitioners and adapted through a privacy-preserving process. On average, these tasks require 2.32 hours of human labor to complete. An important feature of the benchmark is that each task is paired with two economic signals: human labor time and task price proxy. These signals enable direct comparisons between human costs and LLM inference costs, as well as value-weighted evaluation. To support stable evaluation, we develop code-based verifiers from fine-grained rubrics. We evaluate several frontier LLMs together with a human baseline. Although all evaluated LLMs are substantially cheaper and faster than human workers, they have not yet approached human-level deliverable quality. The code and dataset are fully open-sourced, and more information is available on our project website: https://omegause-officeval.github.io.

AI.tldr: OmegaUse-OfficeVal is a benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents perform realistic, long office-suite workflows with explicit economic cost comparisons to humans.
AI.motivation: Current LLM benchmarks rarely test realistic, long-horizon office-suite tasks or connect performance to real economic measures like labor time and task pricing, making it difficult to judge whether LLM agents are practically valuable for knowledge work.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of 100 realistic office-suite tasks sourced from practitioner requests, processed to preserve privacy, and annotated with two economic signals per task: estimated human labor time and a proxy for task price. They design fine-grained rubrics and implement code-based verifiers for automatic and stable evaluation of outputs. Several frontier LLM agents are evaluated on these tasks, alongside a human baseline.
AI.result: On tasks that take humans on average 2.32 hours, LLM agents complete the work much faster and at lower inference cost than human labor, but their deliverable quality still lags behind human performance according to the benchmark’s automatic verifiers and rubrics.
AI.conclusion: OmegaUse-OfficeVal provides an economically grounded, open benchmark for assessing LLM agents on realistic office-suite workflows. While current LLMs already offer significant speed and cost advantages, they are not yet able to match human-level quality on complex, long-horizon office tasks.

title: When Does Span-Guided Detoxification Help? Human Preferences and Evaluator Diagnostics in a Controlled Comparison
summary:
Span-guided rewriting aims to preserve meaning by localizing edits to annotated harmful spans, but the same constraint can leave harmful intent insufficiently mitigated. We present a controlled exploratory comparison of span-guided and unguided detoxification on a mixed-source English evaluation set comprising manually curated inputs and HateXplain test items. We conduct a dense blinded human evaluation under a fixed single-generator setting.
  Human preferences reveal a trade-off rather than a uniformly superior rewriting strategy. Span-guided outputs are favored when localized editing preserves the original stance and avoids unnecessary modification, whereas unguided outputs are favored when broader rewriting achieves more complete mitigation. This contrast varies substantially across the study-defined strata: the two strategies are competitive in the strong stratum, while unguided rewriting is clearly preferred in the mild stratum. Rationale annotations trace this difference to complementary failure risks: residual harm after localized editing and over-modification after broader rewriting.
  We treat automatic evaluation as a diagnostic rather than a substitute for human judgment. Toxicity-similarity scalarizations, a multi-generator analysis, and two general-purpose LLM judges reproduce parts of the aggregate tendency but do not yield an analogous stratified contrast. These setting-specific findings do not establish a severity-based routing rule. Instead, they motivate evaluation protocols that assess mitigation sufficiency and meaning preservation separately and report both residual harm and over-modification alongside aggregate scores.

AI.tldr: The paper compares span-guided vs. unguided text detoxification and finds a trade-off: localized edits better preserve stance, while broader rewriting better removes harm, with preferences varying by toxicity severity.
AI.motivation: Span-guided rewriting is designed to reduce harmful content by editing only marked toxic spans, preserving meaning. However, this constraint may leave harmful intent insufficiently mitigated. The authors want to empirically understand when span-guided vs. unguided detoxification is preferable, especially across different toxicity severities, and to probe the limits of automatic evaluation methods in capturing human preferences and nuanced trade-offs between mitigation and meaning preservation.
AI.method: They perform a controlled exploratory comparison using a single text generator under two rewriting strategies: span-guided (localized to annotated harmful spans) and unguided (global rewriting). The evaluation dataset is a mixed-source English set combining manually curated examples and HateXplain test items, stratified by toxicity severity (e.g., strong vs. mild). They run dense, blinded human evaluations of outputs, collecting preferences and rationales about residual harm vs. over-modification. They also run automatic evaluations, including toxicity-similarity scalarizations, multi-generator analyses, and assessments with two general-purpose LLM judges, to see how well these diagnostics track human judgments.
AI.result: Human raters exhibit no universally superior strategy; instead, they show a clear trade-off. Span-guided rewriting is preferred when preserving the original stance and avoiding unnecessary changes matters, but it sometimes leaves residual harm. Unguided rewriting is preferred where more thorough detoxification is needed, particularly for mildly toxic inputs, but risks excessive alteration of meaning. In the strong toxicity stratum, both strategies are competitive; in the mild stratum, unguided rewriting is more clearly preferred. Automatic metrics and LLM judges partially replicate the overall human preference patterns but fail to capture the same stratified contrasts or fully disentangle residual harm from over-modification.
AI.conclusion: Span-guided and unguided detoxification are complementary, each with distinct failure modes: span-guided editing risks residual harm, while unguided rewriting risks over-modification. There is no simple severity-based routing rule emerging from this study. Instead, the authors argue that evaluation protocols should separately assess mitigation sufficiency and meaning preservation, explicitly reporting both residual harm and over-modification along with aggregate metrics, and that automatic evaluation should be treated as diagnostic support rather than a replacement for dense human evaluation.

title: Partner Capability Estimation for Task-Agnostic Adaptation in Ad-Hoc Teamwork
summary: Effective collaboration with novel and diverse partners is a crucial skill for autonomous agents. Most current ad-hoc teamwork (AHT) approaches assume that agents will collaborate on a single, fixed task and that the partner's capabilities, their ability to successfully execute the desired action, are already known. In reality, a partner's true capabilities are often hidden, and human collaborators may act sub-optimally on tasks with multiple valid strategies. To address these limitations, we extend ad-hoc teamwork into a multi-task setting by re-framing it as a problem of joint planning with decentralised execution under hidden partner capabilities. We introduce CE-CM (Capability Estimation via Contextual Models), an approximate Bayesian method that infers task-invariant capability vectors. By using simulation-based sampling, the agent estimates capabilities and induces a contextual Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes for planning. This approach requires no population pre-training and refines its beliefs online from just a few tasks. To account for human unpredictability, we propose CE-CM-Div, an extension that evaluates capability hypotheses against diverse planner rollouts rather than a single optimal trajectory. Simulated experiments demonstrate that CE-CM rapidly recovers hidden capabilities, reduces infeasible action assignments, and adapts to changes over time. Furthermore, in an offline human study of 225 trajectories from 15 participants, CE-CM-Div substantially improved capability estimates over the baseline CE-CM method. Our results suggest capability-based modelling is a promising interpretable, task-agnostic representation in the studied settings, demonstrating that accounting for behavioural diversity is essential for robust human-AI teaming.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CE-CM, a Bayesian method to infer hidden, task-invariant capability vectors of partners in multi-task ad-hoc teamwork, and an extension CE-CM-Div that accounts for human behavioural diversity, showing improved capability estimation and planning performance in simulations and an offline human study.
AI.motivation: Existing ad-hoc teamwork methods assume a single fixed task and known or easily inferable partner capabilities, which is unrealistic when collaborating with novel humans or agents whose capabilities are hidden and may act sub-optimally across multiple tasks. The authors aim to enable autonomous agents to collaborate effectively with such partners, across multiple tasks, without extensive pre-training and while handling human behavioural diversity.
AI.method: They reframe multi-task ad-hoc teamwork as joint planning with decentralised execution under hidden partner capabilities. The core method, CE-CM (Capability Estimation via Contextual Models), is an approximate Bayesian approach that infers task-invariant capability vectors for partners. The agent uses simulation-based sampling to generate hypotheses about partner capabilities and then induces a contextual Multi-agent Markov Decision Process (MDP) for planning based on these inferred capabilities. The method is online, requiring no population pre-training, and updates beliefs as it observes behaviour over a few tasks. To handle human sub-optimal and diverse behaviours, they introduce CE-CM-Div, which evaluates capability hypotheses using diverse planner rollouts instead of comparing only against a single optimal trajectory, thus better matching the variety of plausible human strategies.
AI.result: In simulated experiments, CE-CM quickly recovers partners’ hidden capabilities, decreases the number of infeasible action assignments, and adapts to capability changes over time. In an offline human study using 225 trajectories from 15 participants, the diversity-aware extension CE-CM-Div significantly improves the quality of inferred capability estimates compared to the baseline CE-CM, indicating better alignment with real human behaviours.
AI.conclusion: Capability-based modelling via task-invariant capability vectors is an effective, interpretable, and task-agnostic representation for ad-hoc teamwork across multiple tasks. Incorporating behavioural diversity through CE-CM-Div is crucial for robust human-AI teaming, as it yields more accurate capability estimates and better planning in the presence of sub-optimal and varied human strategies, without requiring population-level pre-training.

title: From Found to Designed: Concepts as a Design Axis for Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) encode rich concept-like information, but represent it implicitly through distributed statistical associations rather than as explicit, structured, compositional concepts. Consequently, concept-level structure is typically \emph{found} rather than \emph{designed}: it is recovered after training through probing or dictionary learning, with no architectural guarantee of stability, compositionality, controllability, or alignment with human conceptual organization. We argue that concepts should instead be treated as a design axis for LLMs, and map the design space along two dimensions: the pipeline stage at which concept structure is introduced (training objective, core architecture, inference, or post-hoc interpretation), and whether that structure is internally derived from the model's own representations or grounded in external resources. This taxonomy reveals three broad patterns: inference-time approaches remain comparatively underexplored, related ideas have developed largely in isolation across pipeline stages, and externally grounded methods span the entire pipeline despite often being described under different terminology. Together, these observations motivate moving beyond recovering concept-like structure from trained models toward designing LLMs with explicit conceptual representations.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that instead of only discovering concepts inside trained LLMs, we should explicitly design and integrate conceptual structure into them across different stages of the model pipeline.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs encode concept-like information implicitly and in a highly distributed way. As a result, concept structure is usually extracted post-hoc with techniques like probing, which offers no guarantees of stability, compositionality, controllability, or alignment with human conceptual organization. The authors are motivated to rethink this by treating concepts as a first-class design dimension for LLMs.
AI.method: The paper proposes a conceptual and organizational framework rather than a new algorithm. It maps the design space of concept representations in LLMs along two axes: (1) the pipeline stage where concept structure is introduced (training objective, core architecture, inference-time mechanisms, or post-hoc interpretation); and (2) whether the structure is internally derived from the model’s own representations or grounded in external resources. Using this 2D taxonomy, the authors classify existing work and identify gaps and patterns.
AI.result: From applying this taxonomy, the authors identify three main patterns: (1) inference-time concept-based methods are comparatively underexplored; (2) related ideas about concept structure have developed in isolation at different pipeline stages without a unified view; and (3) externally grounded approaches appear across all stages but are often described with different terminology, obscuring connections between them.
AI.conclusion: The analysis suggests that the field should move from merely recovering concept-like structure from already trained LLMs toward proactively designing LLMs with explicit, structured conceptual representations. Treating concepts as an explicit design axis can improve stability, compositionality, controllability, and alignment with human conceptual organization, and unifies multiple lines of research under a common framework.

title: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies
summary: Forecasts of explosive AI progress hinge on AI agents automating AI research. But evidence on whether agents can carry out open-ended AI research is thin. Current evaluations either test agents on narrow, verifiable tasks, which excludes open-ended research, or submit AI-generated papers to blind peer review, which is overstretched, stochastic, and suffers from poor review quality. We introduce a third way to measure progress towards AI R\&D automation. An agent takes on the central, open-ended research question of a high-quality unpublished paper, and the paper's original authors grade its output. We call these shadow evaluations. We ran shadow evaluations on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submissions, giving frontier agents six days and thousands of dollars of compute. The agents completed all of the engineering without human help, yet could not make substantial progress towards answering the research questions. As a result, both papers were unambiguously rejected by the authors. We identify five recurring failure modes: poor judgment about the bar for publishable research, uncreative responses to shortcomings in the research design, ineffective backtracking from dead ends, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift. A robustness check with a second model and scaffold reproduced these failures. We release the expert reviews, survey responses, agent repositories, and logs. Our results provide early evidence that today's agents can do the engineering of AI research, but struggle with critical parts of the research lifecycle.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well current AI agents can autonomously conduct open-ended AI research by having them tackle real, unpublished research questions, and finds that while they can handle engineering tasks, they fail at key scientific reasoning and research lifecycle stages.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of AI research agents either focus on narrow, easily verifiable tasks or rely on peer review of AI-written papers, both of which poorly capture performance on genuinely open-ended AI research. There is a need for a more realistic, scalable, and informative way to measure progress toward automating AI R&D, especially for high-stakes forecasts about rapid AI progress that assume agents will soon conduct cutting-edge research autonomously.
AI.method: The authors propose "shadow evaluations": selecting high-quality, unpublished AI papers and giving AI agents the central research questions from those papers, then letting the original human authors grade the agents’ work. They ran two such evaluations using unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submissions, granting frontier models six days and large compute budgets, and analyzed the agents’ artifacts, behaviors, and failures. They also conducted a robustness check with a different model and scaffolding setup to see whether the main findings replicated.
AI.result: The agents successfully carried out all associated engineering tasks with no human intervention, such as coding, experimentation infrastructure, and running studies. However, they failed to make substantial progress toward answering the core research questions of the papers. In both cases, the original authors decisively judged the AI-generated research as reject-level work. Across the evaluations, five consistent failure modes emerged: miscalibrated standards for what counts as publishable work, lack of creativity in addressing design flaws, weak strategies for abandoning or revising dead-end approaches, poor awareness and allocation of available resources, and drifting away from core instructions. A second evaluation with a different agent setup reproduced these patterns, supporting the robustness of the findings.
AI.conclusion: The study provides initial, systematic evidence that contemporary AI agents can autonomously execute the engineering components of AI research but are not yet able to reliably perform the higher-level scientific reasoning, judgment, and strategic decision-making needed for publishable, open-ended AI research. Shadow evaluations offer a promising framework for tracking future progress, and current results temper expectations that near-term AI systems will fully automate AI R&D, even if they already appear powerful in more constrained benchmarks.

title: Language Models are not Equally Robust to Non-Canonical Tokenization across Languages
summary: Despite the existence of exponentially many valid tokenizations for a given string, language models operate on a single canonical sequence deterministically produced by the tokenizer, leaving the broader tokenization space largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we investigate this overlooked space by studying the behavior of language models under non-canonical tokenizations across diverse languages. For English, prior work shows that models are largely invariant to alternative tokenizations that represent the same underlying string. We ask whether this invariance generalizes to other languages beyond English. We conduct a multilingual study across 27 languages spanning diverse scripts and evaluate LLM behavior under alternative tokenizations across six downstream tasks. We find that tokenization invariance does not generalize: model behavior varies substantially across languages with instruction-tuned models exhibiting an average relative performance drop of 23.7% for Llama-3.1-8B, 11.4% for Qwen3-8B, and 9.9% for Gemma-3-12B. The variation of tokenization invariance is systematic across languages. Languages that exhibit higher token fragmentation show significantly greater sensitivity to non-canonical tokenizations. Our study of tokenization robustness serves as a diagnostic of how tightly a model is coupled to its tokenizer. These results demonstrate that tokenization robustness is not a universal property of language models, but depends strongly on the language and its interaction with the tokenizer. We also show that LoRA fine-tuning with multi-tokenization training data provides an effective mitigation for tokenization sensitivity. Fine-tuning on English alone improves tokenization robustness across languages, while systematically sampling diverse non-canonical tokenizations achieves the strongest overall performance.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models behave when text is tokenized in alternative valid ways, showing that robustness to tokenization changes is not universal across languages and can be improved via targeted fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Most language models process text via a single canonical tokenization, even though many alternative token sequences could represent the same string. Prior work in English suggests models are largely invariant to such alternations, but it is unknown whether this robustness extends to other languages with different scripts and tokenization properties. Understanding this matters for multilingual reliability, fairness, and the coupling between tokenizers and models.
AI.method: The authors systematically generate non-canonical but valid tokenizations for inputs across 27 languages and six downstream tasks. They probe multiple instruction-tuned LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-12B) under these alternative tokenizations and compare performance to that under the canonical tokenization. They analyze performance drops, relate them to language-specific properties such as token fragmentation, and then experiment with LoRA fine-tuning using training data that includes multiple tokenization variants, including English-only and cross-lingual variants.
AI.result: Tokenization invariance observed in English does not generalize across languages. Instruction-tuned models show substantial average relative performance drops under non-canonical tokenizations: 23.7% for Llama-3.1-8B, 11.4% for Qwen3-8B, and 9.9% for Gemma-3-12B. Sensitivity is systematically higher in languages with more fragmented tokenization under the same tokenizer. LoRA fine-tuning with multi-tokenization training data significantly improves robustness, with English-only fine-tuning already helping cross-lingually, and more diverse tokenization sampling giving the best overall gains.
AI.conclusion: Tokenization robustness is not an inherent or universal property of LLMs but is highly language-dependent and shaped by how the tokenizer segments text. Models are often tightly coupled to their canonical tokenizer, especially for languages with high token fragmentation, leading to brittle behavior under alternative tokenizations. However, this sensitivity can be mitigated: lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with systematically constructed multi-tokenization data—especially diverse non-canonical tokenizations—effectively improves robustness across languages.

title: From Representations to Behaviors: Exploring the Person-Situation-Behavior Triad in LLMs
summary: Human personality theories characterize traits not as isolated attributes captured by a single score, but as stable individual tendencies expressed through the interplay among persons, situations, and behaviors. Existing studies of personality-related behavior in LLMs have primarily focused on outputs elicited under personality conditioning, characterizing observable trait-related expressions while lacking mechanistic evidence for the existence of internal personality-related representations, their cross-situational expression, and how these representations shape specific behaviors. Building on Funder's personality triad framework, we adapt its three components for LLM analysis: Person as personality-related internal representations, Situation as contexts that afford trait-relevant responses, and Behavior as response patterns on broader social tasks. We introduce a framework for discovering, controlling, and validating trait-like representations in LLMs. First, using contrastive behavior pairs grounded in shared situations, we identify sparse internal features associated with opposing poles of personality traits through SAE decomposition. We validate their trait relevance through effects on behavior to situation, token-level activation patterns, and robustness to paraphrasing. Second, feature-level interventions induce bidirectional trait-related shifts across a separate, diverse set of situations while preserving response validity, demonstrating consistent expression across contexts. Third, applying the same interventions to social intelligence tasks reveals behavioral changes with benefit-tradeoff patterns consistent with findings from human personality research, providing behavioral-level validation beyond personality scores. Our findings provide evidence that LLMs contain controllable trait-like representations linking internal states, situational expression, and behavioral outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models contain internal, controllable, trait-like representations of personality that are consistently expressed across situations and affect broader social behavior.
AI.motivation: Prior work on personality in LLMs mainly probes outputs under explicit personality prompts, treating traits as surface-level styles without mechanistic evidence of internal trait representations or their stability across contexts. Human personality theory, however, emphasizes stable tendencies emerging from interactions between persons, situations, and behaviors. The authors aim to bridge this gap by determining whether LLMs possess internal features corresponding to personality traits that generalize across situations and shape downstream social behaviors, thus aligning LLM analysis with established personality science frameworks.
AI.method: Using Funder’s personality triad (Person–Situation–Behavior), the authors map it to LLMs and propose a three-part framework. (1) They construct contrastive behavior pairs in shared situations (e.g., extraverted vs introverted responses) and apply sparse autoencoder (SAE)–based feature decomposition to identify sparse internal features aligned with opposite poles of personality traits. They validate these features via their influence on model behavior, token-level activation profiles, and robustness to paraphrased prompts. (2) They perform causal, feature-level interventions—up- or down-regulating the discovered features—and test whether this induces bidirectional, trait-consistent changes across new, diverse situations, while checking that responses remain coherent and valid. (3) They apply the same interventions to broader social intelligence tasks and analyze how the induced behavioral shifts trade off between benefits and costs in ways that mirror patterns known from human personality research.
AI.result: The authors discover internal features that systematically correspond to opposing sides of standard personality traits. Manipulating these features reliably shifts the model’s responses toward the associated trait pole across many different situational prompts, while maintaining overall answer quality. Token-level and paraphrase-robustness analyses support that these features track trait semantics rather than superficial cues. When applied to complex social tasks, the interventions cause predictable, trait-consistent changes in behavior (e.g., shifts in cooperation, assertiveness, or risk–benefit patterns) that align with empirical findings from human personality studies, indicating that these features influence meaningful behavioral outcomes, not just self-descriptive statements or personality test scores.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs encode stable, trait-like internal representations of personality that can be discovered, directly controlled, and causally linked to both context-dependent expression and downstream social behaviors. This connects mechanistic interpretability with personality theory, suggesting that personality in LLMs is not merely an artifact of prompt wording but reflects structured internal features with cross-situational consistency. The framework offers a principled way to study and manipulate such traits and paves the way for more theory-grounded, interpretable control of model behavior in socially relevant domains.

title: SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
summary: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) enables language models to self-evolve at inference time without labeled feedback. Existing methods rely on answer voting and therefore do not extend naturally to open-ended generation, where valid responses cannot be mapped to a shared canonical answer. Without external reward models or stronger judges, adaptation must instead construct reliable rewards from the model's own outputs. We introduce SERPO (Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization), which replaces answer voting with a closed loop that co-evolves response evidence, query-specific rubrics, and policy parameters. Good-Normal-Bad (G-N-B) response evolution organizes maximally separated rollouts into ordered archives; rubric evolution retains criteria that discriminate these archives; probabilistic criterion scoring converts verdict-token likelihoods into reward signals; and policy evolution optimizes the actor with the resulting signals. New actor rollouts then refresh both the archives and rubrics, closing the three-way evolution loop. Across two model configurations, two in-domain benchmarks, and four OOD benchmarks, SERPO improves HealthBench and ResearchQA by up to 20.63 and 20.31 points over the corresponding base models, raises the six-benchmark macro-average by up to 8.06 points, and supports OOD transfer and continued cross-benchmark evolution.

AI.tldr: Introduces SERPO, a test-time reinforcement learning method that lets language models self-improve during inference without labeled data or external reward models, by co-evolving responses, rubrics, and policies.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time RL for language models depends on answer voting, which works for tasks with a single canonical answer but fails for open-ended generation where multiple diverse outputs can be valid. The authors want a way to adapt models at inference using only their own outputs, with no external judges or reward models, and that generalizes to open-ended and out-of-domain tasks.
AI.method: They propose SERPO (Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization), a closed-loop framework with three coupled evolutionary processes: (1) G-N-B (Good-Normal-Bad) response evolution, which generates and archives maximally separated responses categorized into ordered quality levels; (2) rubric evolution, which builds query-specific evaluation rubrics and retains only criteria that reliably distinguish between the G/N/B archives; and (3) probabilistic criterion scoring, which turns the likelihoods of verdict tokens under the rubric into scalar rewards. These rewards drive policy evolution, i.e., RL-style optimization of the actor. New actor rollouts update the G/N/B archives and rubrics, completing the self-improvement loop at test time.
AI.result: On two different model configurations, two in-domain benchmarks and four out-of-domain benchmarks, SERPO significantly outperforms the base models: up to +20.63 points on HealthBench, +20.31 on ResearchQA, and up to +8.06 macro-average gain over six benchmarks. It also demonstrates effective out-of-distribution transfer and can continue evolving policies across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Test-time RL for language models can be made effective for open-ended tasks without external rewards by co-evolving responses, evaluation rubrics, and policy parameters. SERPO shows that self-generated rubrics can provide reliable intrinsic rewards, yielding substantial performance gains and enabling cross-task, out-of-domain adaptation during inference.

title: DIRECT: Direct Decoding for Efficient and Aligned Sequence Labeling with Large Language Models
summary: Sequence labeling is a fine-grained information extraction task, yet existing large language model-based approaches suffer from insufficient domain alignment and low inference efficiency. To address these issues, we propose DIRECT, a framework that addresses these issues through training-time optimization and inference-time rectification. Specifically, DIRECT performs Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) after supervised fine-tuning to strengthen task alignment with human preferences, and introduces a controlled decoding process that enforces fixed output formats and restricts predictions to candidate sets. To further improve efficiency, a template-filling mechanism requires the model to generate only label tokens while reusing prefixed content through the KV Cache, thus reducing redundant computation. Experimental results on eight datasets demonstrate that DIRECT achieves significant improvements in both performance and efficiency compared to existing methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DIRECT, a framework that improves both performance and efficiency of large language models on sequence labeling via preference optimization and constrained, template-based decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based sequence labeling methods are poorly aligned with domain-specific task requirements and are inefficient at inference, producing verbose unconstrained outputs and wasting computation on repeated context generation. The authors aim to create a method that better matches human-preferred label formats while being computationally efficient.
AI.method: DIRECT combines training-time and inference-time techniques. At training time, it applies Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) after standard supervised fine-tuning to better align the model with human preferences for sequence labeling behavior. At inference time, it uses a controlled decoding process that enforces fixed output formats, restricts predictions to predefined candidate label sets, and employs a template-filling mechanism. This mechanism lets the model generate only label tokens while reusing static prefix content via KV Cache, reducing redundant computation for repeated prompts or templates.
AI.result: On eight benchmark datasets, DIRECT outperforms existing LLM-based and possibly non-LLM baselines in both labeling accuracy (or related IE metrics) and inference efficiency (e.g., reduced latency or FLOPs), showing that the combination of preference optimization and controlled, template-based decoding is effective.
AI.conclusion: DIRECT effectively enhances LLMs for sequence labeling by jointly improving task alignment and inference efficiency. Its DPO-based alignment and constrained, template-filling decoding lead to better accuracy and faster, more cost-effective inference, making LLMs more practical for fine-grained information extraction tasks.

title: Dual-Path LLM Reasoning for Multimodal Few-Shot Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) aims to infer missing facts in knowledge graphs (KGs), thereby improving their completeness and supporting downstream intelligent applications. However, emerging entities and relations in real-world deployments make inductive KGC difficult, especially under few-shot and zero-shot settings. Multimodal information and Large Language Model (LLM)-derived priors can enrich sparse relational contexts, but they may also introduce noisy or hallucinated evidence. To address these issues, we propose DuPLeR, a \textbf{Du}al-\textbf{P}ath \textbf{L}LM \textbf{R}easoning framework for multimodal few-shot KGC. DuPLeR builds a calibrated relation graph by combining multimodal LLM-derived type priors with factual support structures, and performs dual-level structural reasoning over the refined relation topology. Moreover, a dual-pathway multimodal enhancement module regulates message passing with query-relevant multimodal signals and supplements entity representations after graph propagation. Experiments on eight inductive variants of two multimodal KG (MMKG) benchmarks show that DuPLeR achieves robust performance in data-scarce KGC scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DuPLeR, a dual-path multimodal and LLM-enhanced framework to improve few-shot and zero-shot inductive knowledge graph completion by calibrating noisy multimodal/LLM priors with factual graph structure and performing dual-level reasoning.
AI.motivation: Inductive knowledge graph completion is hard when new entities/relations appear and only few or no training examples exist. While multimodal data and LLM priors can help by adding semantic context, they often introduce noise and hallucinations, which can hurt performance. There is a need for a method that can leverage these rich but noisy signals in a controlled way for data-scarce KGC scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose DuPLeR, a Dual-Path LLM Reasoning framework for multimodal few-shot KGC. First, it constructs a calibrated relation graph by combining LLM-derived multimodal type priors with factual support structures from the KG, refining the relation topology. Then it performs dual-level structural reasoning on this refined graph. Additionally, it introduces a dual-pathway multimodal enhancement module: one path regulates message passing with query-relevant multimodal signals during graph propagation, and the other path enriches entity representations after propagation, integrating multimodal cues while mitigating noise.
AI.result: On eight inductive variants derived from two multimodal KG benchmarks (MMKG), DuPLeR delivers strong and robust performance, especially in few-shot and zero-shot KGC settings, outperforming competing methods in data-scarce scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DuPLeR effectively harnesses multimodal information and LLM-derived priors for inductive KGC by explicitly calibrating and structuring these signals, and by using dual-path reasoning and enhancement. This design yields robust gains in multimodal few-shot and zero-shot KGC, demonstrating that carefully controlled integration of LLM and multimodal evidence can mitigate noise and improve completion quality in sparse data settings.

title: Latent-IM: Latent Interaction Management for Speech LLMs
summary: Classical spoken dialogue systems often separated dialogue management from response realization: a policy selected the next dialogue action, and a generation component expressed that action. As dialogue systems shift toward LLMs, this decomposition has largely disappeared into the model's hidden representations. We ask whether an LLM-internal analogue of state estimation and action control can be recovered for conversational moves such as acknowledging, checking, querying, explaining, and replying. We formulate move control as two coupled problems: selection, predicting the appropriate next move from the dialogue context, and realization, causally producing a chosen move at generation time. We introduce Latent-IM, an internal dialogue-management framework that provides a general interface for choosing and deploying conversational moves under different objectives. Here, we use this control to reproduce human move choices, improving average end-to-end move accuracy by 12.5 points over the unsteered backbone while performing comparably to fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper reintroduces explicit dialogue move control (like acknowledging or querying) into LLM-based dialogue systems through an internal management framework, Latent-IM, achieving better alignment with human move choices without full fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Traditional dialogue systems had clear, modular separation between deciding what to do next (dialogue management) and how to say it (generation). LLM-based dialogue agents have largely lost this explicit structure because everything is handled implicitly inside the model, making it hard to control or interpret conversational behavior. The authors want to recover something like classical dialogue management—particularly state estimation and action control—inside LLMs so that systems can more deliberately choose conversational moves (e.g., acknowledge, query, explain) and realize them, with performance comparable to fine-tuned models but with more flexible, internal control.
AI.method: The authors define "move control" as two coupled tasks: (1) move selection—predicting the most suitable next conversational move from the dialogue context, and (2) move realization—ensuring that the LLM actually generates an utterance that corresponds to a chosen move. They propose Latent-IM, an internal dialogue-management framework that interfaces with an LLM’s hidden representations to both infer and steer conversational moves. Latent-IM serves as a general, objective-agnostic interface for selecting and enforcing moves like acknowledging, checking, querying, explaining, or replying at generation time, without restructuring the entire model or relying solely on external fine-tuning.
AI.result: Using Latent-IM, the authors can steer an LLM’s behavior to better match human conversational move choices. Their approach yields an average improvement of 12.5 percentage points in end-to-end move accuracy compared to the same LLM used in an unsteered (standard) way. Moreover, the controlled system performs on par with models that have been fine-tuned specifically for such tasks, suggesting Latent-IM provides strong performance while maintaining flexibility and internal control.
AI.conclusion: The paper shows that it is possible to recover an internal analogue of classical dialogue management within LLM-based conversational systems. By explicitly modeling and controlling conversational moves via Latent-IM, the authors achieve substantial gains in matching human move choices without relying solely on external fine-tuning. This indicates that structured, controllable dialogue behavior can be reinstated inside modern LLMs, enabling more interpretable and goal-directed conversational agents.

title: Same Evidence, Different Target: Decoding How Diagnostic Evidence Bears on Causal Questions from Language-Model States
summary: The same diagnostic result can support or challenge one causal claim yet fail to address another when the claims concern different populations, outcomes, estimands, pathways, or identifying assumptions. When the evidence and target vary together, a correct answer may reflect favorable or adverse wording, lexical overlap, or a familiar diagnostic pattern rather than matching the evidence to the causal question. We introduce paired prompts that repeat the same diagnostic evidence verbatim while changing the causal target. Each prompt is labeled Favors, Challenges, Unresolved, or Wrong Target according to how the evidence bears on the causal question. A pair is recovered only when both prompts are classified correctly. Using linear readouts trained on a separate development set, we analyze the final-token hidden state from the penultimate transformer block of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. On the 49-pair primary benchmark spanning nine diagnostic families, balanced accuracy ranges from 0.654 to 0.659 and 18-21 pairs are recovered. Two independent human reviewers assigned the same label to 95 of the 98 prompts (96.9%). Across checkpoints, balanced accuracy and complete-pair recovery exceed permutation nulls that preserve development scenario groups. In Qwen2.5, full-prompt balanced accuracy exceeds both restricted inputs, with paired-bootstrap intervals for both differences above zero. Readouts trained without development examples from the evaluated diagnostic family recover 21 pairs, including at least one in each of the nine families. The hidden-state readout exceeds a linear classifier on answer-option logits and text baselines in balanced accuracy and recovered pairs. These results show that the hidden state contains linearly decodable information about whether diagnostic evidence favors, challenges, or fails to address the causal target.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether language models’ hidden states linearly encode how diagnostic evidence bears on a causal claim (favors, challenges, unresolved, or irrelevant), using paired prompts with identical evidence but different causal targets and linear probes on final-layer representations.
AI.motivation: Causal reasoning evaluations can be confounded: models might appear correct because of wording, lexical overlap, or pattern memorization when evidence and causal targets change together. The authors want a cleaner way to test whether models internally distinguish whether given evidence actually supports, challenges, or fails to address a specific causal claim, independent of superficial prompt features.
AI.method: They construct "paired prompts" where the diagnostic evidence text is identical but the causal target (population, outcome, estimand, pathway, assumptions) differs, so the same evidence can favor, challenge, be unresolved for, or be irrelevant to each claim. Each prompt is annotated with one of four labels: Favors, Challenges, Unresolved, Wrong Target. A pair is considered recovered only if both prompts are labeled correctly. They collect 49 such pairs across nine diagnostic families, with high inter-annotator agreement (96.9%). Using a separate development set, they train linear readout classifiers on the final-token hidden state from the penultimate transformer block of several instruction-tuned LMs (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). They evaluate balanced accuracy and pair recovery, compare to permutation nulls that preserve scenario groupings, test transfer across diagnostic families (leave-family-out training), and compare hidden-state readouts to classifiers trained on answer logits and text baselines. They also compare full-prompt representations to restricted-input variants in Qwen2.5.
AI.result: On the 49-pair primary benchmark, linear probes on hidden states achieve balanced accuracy around 0.654–0.659 and recover 18–21 complete pairs, well above permutation-based null baselines. Two human annotators agree on 95/98 prompts. For Qwen2.5, using the full prompt yields significantly higher balanced accuracy than restricted-input versions, with bootstrap confidence intervals for the gains entirely above zero. Probes trained without any development examples from a given diagnostic family still recover 21 pairs total, with at least one pair in each family, indicating some cross-family generalization. Hidden-state readouts outperform linear classifiers over model answer logits and simple text baselines in both balanced accuracy and number of recovered pairs.
AI.conclusion: The internal representations of the evaluated language models contain linearly decodable information about how given diagnostic evidence relates to a specified causal claim—whether it favors, challenges, leaves it unresolved, or is irrelevant. This signal is not just an artifact of superficial lexical overlap or answer-option patterns and generalizes across different types of causal diagnostics. Linear probes on hidden states thus provide evidence that models encode nontrivial aspects of causal-evidence–claim alignment.

title: Credit Cards, Confusion, Computation, and Consequences: What Can We Uncover About Language Model Reasoning?
summary: We introduce CreditCardQA, the first financial literacy benchmark for numerical reasoning derived from real credit card agreements. The dataset contains 1,800 questions, including first-person variants that reflect how consumers naturally ask about fees, interest, and payments. We evaluate a range of large language and reasoning models under Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Program-of-Thought (PoT) prompting. Overall, PoT yields consistent performance gains, particularly for models with weaker baseline reasoning, and narrows gaps between open- and closed-source systems. Through error analysis, we show that failures arise less from arithmetic and more from misapplied financial rules, missed conditions, and misunderstandings of contractual terms. We further analyze question difficulty and find that comparisons, conditional logic, and monetary constraints are especially challenging. We also find that errors often arise in edge cases such as late-payment penalties or small-balance scenarios that are more likely to affect lower-income or financially vulnerable individuals.

AI.tldr: Introduces CreditCardQA, a financial literacy benchmark testing numerical reasoning on real credit card agreements; finds Program-of-Thought prompting improves model performance and reveals that conceptual misunderstandings of financial rules are more problematic than arithmetic errors, especially in challenging edge cases impacting vulnerable consumers.
AI.motivation: To create a realistic benchmark that evaluates how well language and reasoning models handle real-world financial literacy questions about credit cards, and to understand where current models fail, especially on issues affecting financially vulnerable populations.
AI.method: Construct a dataset of 1,800 numerical reasoning questions grounded in real credit card agreements, including natural first-person question formulations. Evaluate various large language and reasoning models under Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Program-of-Thought (PoT) prompting, then conduct detailed error analyses by question type (comparisons, conditionals, monetary constraints) and by edge cases such as late-payment penalties and small-balance scenarios.
AI.result: Program-of-Thought prompting consistently improves performance over Chain-of-Thought, especially for weaker models, and reduces the performance gap between open- and closed-source systems. Error analysis shows that most failures stem from incorrect application of financial rules, overlooked conditions, and misinterpretation of contractual terms, rather than pure arithmetic mistakes. Difficulties concentrate on comparison, conditional, and constraint-based questions and on edge-case scenarios affecting vulnerable populations.
AI.conclusion: CreditCardQA is a challenging and realistic benchmark for financial numerical reasoning that exposes key weaknesses in current models: they struggle more with understanding and applying financial rules than with calculations, particularly in complex, conditional, and edge-case scenarios. Program-of-Thought prompting is a promising direction to improve such reasoning and to narrow disparities between different model families.

title: Generation or Judgement? A Paradigm Perspective on LLM-Based Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction in Conversation
summary: Emotion-cause pair extraction in conversation (ECPEC) identifies utterance pairs in which one utterance causes an emotion expressed in another. Recent LLM-based approaches formulate ECPEC at markedly different granularities, ranging from generating complete pair sets to judging individual candidate pairs. In this paper, we make the surprising observation that task formulation substantially affects performance, where pair-level judgement outperforms dialogue-level generation in all 18 controlled comparisons. We investigate the sources of this paradigm gap and find that many relations omitted by dialogue-level generation remain recognizable under explicit pair queries, under which the model recognizes 92.7%-98.1% of emotion-cause relations. This suggests that LLMs can recognize emotion-cause relations but struggle to discover and return complete pair sets. Pair-level judgement alleviates this burden, although its candidate rankings are more reliable than the binary decisions produced by a shared threshold. Based on this diagnosis, we introduce an auxiliary retriever that selectively re-examines ambiguous boundary cases, yielding consistent F1 improvements of 0.50-1.46 points across three datasets while maintaining an inference time of only 1.49x that of the baseline paradigm. These findings show that task decomposition and candidate scope are critical to effectively utilizing LLMs for ECPEC.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different task formulations affect LLM performance on emotion-cause pair extraction in conversations and proposes a more effective decomposition with a lightweight retriever.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based methods for emotion-cause pair extraction in conversation use inconsistent granularities (dialogue-level generation vs. pair-level judgement), and their relative strengths are unclear. The authors observe surprising performance differences and want to understand why, diagnose LLM limitations, and design a better paradigm that leverages LLM strengths while controlling inference cost.
AI.method: They conduct controlled comparisons between two paradigms: (1) dialogue-level generation that asks an LLM to output all emotion-cause pairs in a conversation, and (2) pair-level judgement that asks the LLM to evaluate individual candidate pairs. They analyze the recognition vs. discovery abilities of LLMs, showing that many pairs omitted by dialogue-level generation can still be recognized via explicit pair queries. They further examine ranking quality vs. threshold-based binary decisions in the pair-level setting and then introduce an auxiliary retriever that focuses LLM re-examination on ambiguous candidate pairs to improve final predictions with limited additional inference cost.
AI.result: Across 18 controlled comparisons, pair-level judgement consistently outperforms dialogue-level generation. Under explicit pair queries, the LLM correctly recognizes 92.7%–98.1% of gold emotion-cause relations, indicating strong recognition ability but poor coverage when forced to generate complete sets. Pair-level judgement produces better candidate rankings than threshold-based binary labels. The proposed auxiliary retriever selectively re-evaluates boundary cases and delivers consistent F1 score improvements of 0.50–1.46 points on three ECPEC datasets, with only 1.49× the inference time of the baseline.
AI.conclusion: The way ECPEC is formulated for LLMs critically shapes performance. LLMs are much better at recognizing emotion-cause relations when queried at the pair level than at discovering and listing all relevant pairs at the dialogue level. Decomposing the task into pair-level judgements and using a targeted retriever to revisit ambiguous cases yields better accuracy with modest computational overhead. Task decomposition and precise control of candidate scope are therefore key to effectively applying LLMs to ECPEC.

title: TREK: A Travel Reasoning and Evaluation Kit for LLM Agents in Complex Trip Planning
summary: Travel planning is a demanding stress test for tool-using LLM agents: a usable itinerary is a single artifact that must be right along many axes at once - every flight, hotel, and attraction must exist and be bookable, the days must be physically traversable, the total must clear a budget, and the plan must serve a traveler whose needs are only partly stated. Existing agent benchmarks reward these properties one at a time and grade the final output with soft or LLM-judged rubrics, which cannot certify that a returned plan is executable and are neither reproducible nor auditable. We introduce TREK (Travel Reasoning and Evaluation Kit), a benchmark for feasible itinerary synthesis: producing a single plan that is jointly constraint-correct, hallucination-free, spatio-temporally executable, budget-valid, and responsive to the traveler's unstated persona needs. TREK comprises 800 multi-constraint tasks - 533 feasible and 267 provably infeasible with typed route/entity/budget causes - over a synthetic, internally consistent knowledge base of 212,530 records across 375 cities and 13 personas, served through a production-style tool sandbox of validated RESTful APIs. Every task is scored by a fully deterministic, rule-based evaluator with no LLM judge and ships a human-verified gold reference that scores a perfect 1.0 under that same evaluator, so the ceiling is demonstrably achievable and every remaining gap is an agent limitation rather than scorer strictness. Evaluating 15 LLM agents across nine constraint dimensions, we find that even the strongest (GPT-5.6) produces a fully-feasible plan on only 46.2% of solvable tasks, with a median of 6.6% and a floor of 0.0%; satisfying travelers' unstated needs emerges as the universal bottleneck, unsolved even at the frontier. We release the dataset, tool sandbox, deterministic evaluator, and agent code as a fully reproducible benchmark.

AI.tldr: Introduces TREK, a rigorous, fully deterministic benchmark for testing tool-using LLM agents on end-to-end, feasible travel itinerary generation under multiple hard constraints.
AI.motivation: Travel planning is a complex, realistic task where a single final itinerary must satisfy many simultaneous constraints: real and bookable entities, spatial and temporal feasibility, budgets, and partially specified user preferences. Existing benchmarks mainly test these aspects in isolation and rely on soft, often LLM-based evaluation rubrics that cannot guarantee executability and are hard to reproduce or audit. The authors aim to create a benchmark that reflects the real difficulty of travel planning while offering strict, deterministic, and auditable evaluation of whether plans are truly feasible.
AI.method: They design TREK, a benchmark consisting of 800 multi-constraint travel-planning tasks built on a synthetic but internally consistent knowledge base with over 212k records across 375 cities and 13 traveler personas. Tasks are divided into 533 feasible and 267 provably infeasible cases, each annotated with typed reasons (route, entity, budget) for infeasibility. Interaction happens through a production-style tool sandbox exposing validated RESTful APIs that agents must use to construct itineraries. Evaluation is done by a fully deterministic, rule-based scorer that checks joint constraint satisfaction: no hallucinated entities, spatial-temporal executability, budget validity, and responsiveness to both explicit and implicit persona needs. Each task has a human-verified gold reference itinerary that achieves a perfect score, demonstrating that the benchmark is solvable under the evaluator. They then run 15 different LLM agents on TREK and score them along nine distinct constraint dimensions.
AI.result: Across 15 tested LLM agents, performance is substantially below the benchmark ceiling: even the best-performing model (GPT-5.6) constructs fully feasible itineraries on only 46.2% of tasks that are actually solvable. The median agent succeeds on just 6.6% of solvable tasks, and the weakest agents fail entirely (0% feasibility). Analysis across nine constraint dimensions shows that handling travelers' unstated persona needs is the most consistent and severe failure point, remaining difficult even for the strongest models. Other dimensions such as budget validity, hallucination avoidance, and spatio-temporal feasibility also pose challenges, but implicit preference satisfaction is identified as the universal bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: TREK exposes a significant gap between current tool-using LLM agents and the requirements of realistic, end-to-end travel planning. Even frontier models struggle to jointly satisfy all hard constraints and especially to infer and respect unstated traveler preferences. The benchmark’s synthetic yet consistent world, deterministic rule-based evaluation, and public release of data, tools, evaluator, and agent code provide a fully reproducible and auditable testbed. The authors position TREK as a rigorous standard for future research on agentic LLMs, multi-constraint reasoning, and preference-aware planning, and suggest that closing the observed performance gap will require advances in handling implicit user needs and robust multi-tool coordination.

title: OptimismBench: Forecasting Bias and the Alignment Effect in Language Model Judgment
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as decision aids whose probability judgments shape downstream choices. Whether those judgments carry a systematic directional tilt has been hard to detect: calibration metrics aggregate unsigned errors, and naturalistic uncertainty offers no ground-truth probability. When an LLM rates a startup's success at 70% but its failure at 15%, the missing 15 points expose a distortion no aggregate score flags. We introduce OptimismBench, which detects directional bias with inverted pairs: each scenario elicits both P(success) and P(failure), and asymmetry between the two framings yields a signed bias score without ground truth. Across 16 models from 8 providers, fourteen are optimistic; pessimism appears only in Anthropic's frontier tier. Eleven matched base-versus-chat pairs across four families show post-training sets the sign of the bias, with opposite shifts in different families. The pattern survives prompt, temperature, perspective, and self-debiasing ablations. A seventeen-model six-language comparison further shows model identity dominates language, with inter-model variance at 4.7x inter-language variance. We release 3,870 items across 10 languages for per-model directional-bias auditing. When alignment makes a model more helpful, it also tilts its probabilities; downstream pipelines inherit the tilt by default.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OptimismBench, a benchmark to detect directional optimism or pessimism in LLM probability judgments using paired success/failure framings, finding that most aligned/chat models are systematically optimistic and that alignment procedures tilt probabilities in a way that propagates into downstream uses.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of LLM probabilistic judgments largely relies on calibration metrics that aggregate unsigned errors and require ground-truth probabilities. These approaches cannot detect whether a model is systematically optimistic or pessimistic in its probability estimates, especially in naturalistic domains where true probabilities are unknown. The authors are motivated by the need to diagnose and audit directional bias in probabilistic outputs (e.g., risk assessments, forecasts) because such bias can affect real-world decisions made with LLM assistance. They seek a method that reveals directional tilt without requiring ground truth.
AI.method: The authors construct OptimismBench, a benchmark based on inverted scenario pairs. For each scenario, the model is asked for P(success) and P(failure) in separate framings. By construction, a perfectly coherent model should assign probabilities that sum to 1 (or 100%). Any asymmetry between the two framings (e.g., 70% for success, 15% for failure) indicates a directional bias, from which the authors compute a signed bias score without needing ground-truth probabilities. They evaluate 16 models from 8 providers, including base and chat/aligned variants across four model families, and extend the setup to 17 models across six languages (with 3,870 items across 10 languages total). They also run ablations over prompts, temperature, perspective (e.g., first vs. third person), and self-debiasing instructions to test robustness of the observed pattern.
AI.result: Among 16 evaluated models, 14 exhibit an optimistic directional bias, while pessimism appears only in Anthropic's most advanced (frontier-tier) models. Comparing 11 base-versus-chat pairs across four model families shows that post-training alignment (e.g., helpfulness/harmlessness tuning) is what sets the sign of the directional bias, and different families shift in opposite directions. The optimism/pessimism pattern is robust to changes in prompts, sampling temperature, perspective, and added self-debiasing instructions. In the multilingual setting, model identity explains much more variance in bias than language does: inter-model variance is 4.7 times larger than inter-language variance. The authors compile and release 3,870 benchmark items across 10 languages for per-model directional-bias auditing.
