AI.conclusion: OptimismBench reveals that many LLMs have systematic directional bias—typically optimism—in their probability judgments, even when they may appear well-calibrated by conventional metrics. Alignment procedures that make models more helpful also tend to tilt their probabilities, and this tilt varies by model family. Because downstream decision pipelines that rely on LLM probabilities will inherit this directional bias by default, the authors argue for explicit auditing and mitigation of such bias. The released benchmark provides a practical tool for developers and users to measure and monitor optimism/pessimism in LLM probabilistic reasoning across models and languages.

title: Evaluating Regional Bias in LLMs From Abstract Stereotype to Concrete Social Decision-Making
summary: Regional bias in large language models (LLMs) may shape both perceptions of regional groups and decisions about individuals from different regions. Yet existing studies often examine these manifestations separately, leaving their structure and consequences unclear. We introduce Stereotypes-to-Decisions (S2D), a systematic framework evaluating regional bias from abstract stereotypes to concrete social decisions. Covering all 34 provincial-level administrative regions of China, S2D evaluates six LLMs using stereotype ratings of Warmth (perceived friendliness and trustworthiness) and Competence (perceived capability and intelligence), along with paired-choice tasks across Education, Occupation, and Social Interaction. Results reveal substantial regional differences in regional scores, with considerable agreement across models, especially for Competence and Occupation decisions. Furthermore, these patterns are associated with regional economic and digital development indicators and display mixed human-like stereotypes, with some regions rated highly on one dimension but poorly on the other. They also remain largely stable across Chinese and English prompts. Overall, our findings show that regional bias in LLMs is prevalent, systematic, and consequential, motivating more regionally aware evaluation and mitigation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework (S2D) to systematically measure regional bias in LLMs for all 34 provincial regions of China, from abstract stereotypes (warmth, competence) to concrete decisions (education, occupation, social interaction), finding consistent, economically-linked, and largely language-invariant biases across multiple models.
AI.motivation: Existing work on bias in LLMs often treats stereotypes and downstream decisions separately, making it hard to understand how abstract regional impressions translate into concrete, potentially harmful choices. There is also little comprehensive, region-level analysis (across all Chinese provinces) of how LLMs encode and apply regional stereotypes, and how those correlate with real-world indicators or human stereotypes. To address the gap, the authors aim to build a unified evaluation framework that links stereotype dimensions to consequential decisions and compares multiple models systematically.
AI.method: The authors design the Stereotypes-to-Decisions (S2D) framework, which: (1) defines stereotype ratings along two social-psychological dimensions—Warmth (friendliness, trustworthiness) and Competence (capability, intelligence); (2) constructs evaluation tasks for all 34 provincial-level regions of China; (3) runs six different LLMs on (a) rating tasks for warmth and competence, and (b) paired-choice tasks where the model must pick between regions in scenarios related to education, occupation, and social interaction; (4) measures regional scores, cross-model agreement, and how decisions align with stereotype dimensions; (5) analyzes correlations with regional economic and digital development indicators; (6) compares responses across Chinese vs. English prompts to test language robustness.
AI.result: The study finds large regional differences in LLM-assigned warmth and competence scores, and in which regions are favored in different decision scenarios. There is notable consistency across the six models, particularly for competence ratings and occupation-related choices. The pattern of regional scores correlates with objective indicators of economic and digital development, and the overall structure of stereotypes resembles mixed human-like impressions, where some regions are high in competence but low in warmth and vice versa. These biases are largely stable regardless of whether prompts are in Chinese or English, indicating language-independent encoding of regional stereotypes.
AI.conclusion: Regional bias in LLMs is not random or marginal; it is extensive, structured, and meaningfully linked to both abstract stereotypes and concrete decisions. Because these patterns align with socio-economic indicators and show cross-model and cross-language stability, they likely reflect deep-seated, human-like stereotype structures. The work underscores the need for evaluation and mitigation methods that explicitly account for regional dimensions of bias, especially when LLM outputs may affect perceptions or decisions about individuals from different regions.

title: DenseOn with the LateOn: Fully Open Dense and Late-Interaction Models for Multilingual, Long-Context, and Code Search
summary: State-of-the-art retrieval models increasingly rely on closed training data, creating a reproducibility gap. We present an open end-to-end recipe for training retrieval models and study how English supervision transfers to multilingual retrieval through translate-train. We first reconstruct and curate 665M English contrastive pre-training pairs from 1.4B pairs across 34 public sources and build 1.88M supervised fine-tuning pairs with mined hard negatives. Training yields two 149M-parameter models: DenseOn, a single-vector dense model, and LateOn, a ColBERT-style late-interaction model. They achieve 56.20 and 57.22 average nDCG@10 on BEIR, respectively, setting new state-of-the-art results for this size class. We then translate the validated English data into eight languages, yielding 2.8B pairs with cross-lingual samples, and train mDenseOn and mLateOn, two 307M-parameter models built on mmBERT-base. Despite sharing their backbone, data, and objectives, their representations behave differently: the dense model is strong on English and translated languages but degrades outside translate-train support, whereas the late-interaction model generalizes better to unseen languages and scripts. This suggests that token-level matching turns translate-train from a target-language expansion strategy into a multilingual generalization recipe. We publicly release the models, datasets, and training code.

AI.tldr: They build fully open, reproducible dense and late-interaction retrieval models from large-scale public English data, then extend them via translation to multilingual settings, analyzing how architecture affects cross-lingual generalization.
AI.motivation: Modern top retrieval models rely on private or undisclosed training data, making them hard to reproduce or extend, and it is unclear how well English-only supervision can be leveraged to build strong multilingual retrievers in an open, transparent way.
AI.method: (1) Aggregate 1.4B English contrastive pairs from 34 public sources, filter them into 665M high-quality pre-training pairs; (2) construct 1.88M supervised finetuning pairs with hard negatives; (3) train two 149M-parameter retrieval models—a single-vector dense model (DenseOn) and a ColBERT-style late-interaction model (LateOn); (4) evaluate them on BEIR; (5) translate the curated English training data into 8 languages, including cross-lingual pairs, yielding 2.8B training pairs; (6) train two 307M-parameter multilingual versions (mDenseOn, mLateOn) on an mmBERT-base backbone and compare their behavior on seen vs unseen languages and scripts.
AI.result: DenseOn and LateOn reach 56.20 and 57.22 average nDCG@10 on BEIR, achieving new state-of-the-art performance for ~150M-parameter models. In the multilingual setting, mDenseOn excels on English and languages present in translate-train data but degrades for unseen languages, while mLateOn exhibits better generalization to unseen languages and scripts despite identical backbone, data, and objectives.
AI.conclusion: An entirely open pipeline can produce competitive retrieval models using only public data. Translate-train is highly effective for multilingual retrieval, but architectural choices matter: late-interaction (token-level) models translate English supervision into more robust cross-lingual generalization than dense single-vector models, indicating that fine-grained token matching is key to scaling translate-train beyond just target-language coverage.

title: Pangram 4 Technical Report
summary: We present Pangram 4, the latest deep-learning-based AI-text classification model from Pangram Labs. We achieve an AUROC of 0.9916 with a false positive rate of 0.0041% and a false negative rate of 0.3396%. In addition to its increased overall accuracy compared with Pangram 3, Pangram 4 exhibits superior out-of-distribution generalization and robustness to adversarial attacks. Another novel contribution of Pangram 4 is its improved ability to distinguish fine-grained edits and mixed AI-human co-authored text. We demonstrate improvements to both boundary detection tasks and the detection of interleaved AI assistance. Finally, we report metrics on standard AI detection benchmarks showing that Pangram 4 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the AI text detection task across a wide variety of settings and domains.

AI.tldr: Pangram 4 is a new deep-learning AI-text detector that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, strong robustness, and better handling of mixed human–AI writing.
AI.motivation: As AI language models become widespread, distinguishing AI-generated text from human-written content is increasingly important for tasks like academic integrity, content moderation, and platform trust. Previous models (e.g., Pangram 3) had limitations in accuracy, robustness to adversarial attacks, and difficulty handling nuanced cases such as small edits or mixed human–AI co-authorship. The paper aims to address these gaps by building a more accurate and robust AI-text classifier that works reliably across domains and text types.
AI.method: The authors design Pangram 4 as a deep-learning-based AI-text classification model. They train and evaluate it on large datasets of AI-generated, human-written, and mixed/co-authored texts, including out-of-distribution samples and adversarially modified texts. The model is optimized to reduce both false positives and false negatives, and to better detect fine-grained boundaries between human and AI segments, including interleaved assistance. They benchmark Pangram 4 on standard AI detection benchmarks and compare it to previous versions and competing systems.
AI.result: Pangram 4 achieves an AUROC of 0.9916, with a very low false positive rate (0.0041%) and a low false negative rate (0.3396%). It outperforms Pangram 3 in overall accuracy and shows superior out-of-distribution generalization and robustness to adversarial attacks. It is better at detecting fine-grained edits and distinguishing AI from human text in mixed, co-authored documents. On standard AI detection benchmarks, Pangram 4 reaches state-of-the-art performance across diverse settings and domains.
AI.conclusion: Pangram 4 sets a new state of the art for AI text detection, combining high accuracy with robustness and improved handling of complex, mixed-authorship scenarios. The model advances boundary detection and interleaved AI-assistance detection, making it a stronger and more general tool for identifying AI involvement in text across many domains.

title: APEX-Accounting
summary: We introduce APEX-Accounting, a benchmark built by Mercor in partnership with Ramp, to assess whether frontier models can do the real work of accountants. Tasks include reconciling accounts, accruing expenses, posting transactions, and producing reports. The private eval set comprises 160 tasks, split across 10 worlds. Each world contains an accounting system, as well as spreadsheets, PDFs, and other files. Every task was authored and solved by experts in accounting and bookkeeping, who also wrote grading rubrics. Across nine frontier models, Claude-Fable-5 (Max) leads with 56.4% Mean Criteria@3, ahead of Muse-Spark-1.1 (xHigh) at 52.6%. No model scores more than 2.6% Pass^8 (GPT-5.6-Sol (Max+Pro)) and the highest Pass@8 is 21.5% (Muse-Spark-1.1 (xHigh)). We experiment with increasing the token budget from $1 to $50 and observe an instance of Simpson's paradox: scores increase as the token budget increases but within a given budget-constrained harness, scores are lower on tasks where the model spends more tokens. As APEX-Accounting is a closed benchmark, leaderboard evals can be run for any frontier model on request.

AI.tldr: APEX-Accounting is a closed, expert‑built benchmark that tests whether frontier AI models can perform realistic accounting workflows. Current top models perform moderately but are still far from reliably handling full accounting tasks.
AI.motivation: To move beyond toy problems and evaluate whether leading AI models can handle end‑to‑end, real‑world accounting work such as reconciliation, accruals, transaction posting, and reporting. Existing benchmarks often miss the complexity of practical accounting workflows with multiple documents, systems, and expert‑defined rubrics, so there is a need for a realistic, professionally curated evaluation suite.
AI.method: The authors construct APEX-Accounting, a private benchmark of 160 tasks grouped into 10 “worlds,” each world simulating a realistic accounting environment with an accounting system plus associated artifacts (spreadsheets, PDFs, and other files). Expert accountants and bookkeepers design the tasks, provide correct solutions, and write detailed grading rubrics. They then evaluate nine frontier LLMs on these tasks using metrics such as Mean Criteria@3, Pass^8, and Pass@8, and also run experiments varying the token budget from $1 to $50 to study how performance changes with allowed context/compute usage per task.
AI.result: Among nine tested frontier models, Claude-Fable-5 (Max) achieves the best Mean Criteria@3 at 56.4%, followed by Muse-Spark-1.1 (xHigh) at 52.6%. However, absolute pass rates remain low: the best Pass^8 is only 2.6% (GPT-5.6-Sol (Max+Pro)), and the best Pass@8 is 21.5% (Muse-Spark-1.1 (xHigh)), indicating that models rarely fully solve tasks to expert standards. When increasing token budgets from $1 to $50, aggregate scores rise, but within any fixed budget setting, tasks on which models consume more tokens tend to have lower scores, illustrating Simpson’s paradox in this evaluation setup.
AI.conclusion: APEX-Accounting provides a rigorous, realistic, and expert‑curated benchmark for testing whether AI models can perform genuine accounting workflows. Current frontier models show partial competence but remain far from reliably executing end‑to‑end accounting tasks at professional quality, even with generous token budgets. The benchmark will be maintained as a closed, request‑based leaderboard resource for evaluating new frontier models and for studying how factors like token budget impact performance on complex, document‑heavy accounting tasks.

title: Mental World Modeling
summary: World models enable a predictive substrate for planning and action, yet existing formulations merely answer a physical question: what/where it is, and how will it evolve. Human behavior, however, is driven by hidden mental state (what a person believes, wants, intends, feels, and considers socially permissible), so a model that tracks the physical scene but not what each agent knows and believes about it predicts the wrong action for the right-looking scene. We formulate Mental World Modeling (MWM), a generic theoretical framework that makes mental variables core components of a world model rather than posthoc rationales: MWM aintains a coupled physical-mental world state, renders a target-specific partial observation, and simulates how candidate actions jointly update both components. We instantiate the framework in MENTIS, a training-free and fully inspectable baseline that decomposes the process into state parsing, target-observation generation, action decomposition, coupled physical and mental transition, and branch-level value evaluation. On a manually constructed, quality-controlled dataset of situated decision scenarios spanning text, image, and sounding-video stories, experiments with 8 modern LLM-based world models demonstrate that explicitly modeling the mental state is essential for predicting human decisions. Deeper analyses further expose the bottlenecks of current mental world modeling. We expect MWM as a next stage of world modeling, from simulating physical scenes to simulating the minds that act in them.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mental World Modeling (MWM), a framework that extends world models to explicitly represent agents’ mental states (beliefs, desires, intentions, social norms) alongside physical states, showing that this is crucial for accurately predicting human decisions.
AI.motivation: Conventional world models focus on physical states—objects, locations, and their dynamics—and thus answer only “what is where and how will it move?”. However, human behavior depends critically on hidden mental states such as beliefs, desires, intentions, emotions, and perceptions of social norms. A system that only models the physical scene but ignores what each agent knows, believes, or wants will often mispredict actions: it will foresee the wrong behavior even in a visually correct scene. The paper is motivated by the need to elevate mental states from post-hoc explanations to first-class variables within world models, enabling better prediction and understanding of human decisions across modalities (text, images, video).
AI.method: The authors propose Mental World Modeling (MWM), a theoretical framework in which the world state is explicitly split into coupled physical and mental components. MWM defines: (1) a joint physical-mental state representation; (2) a mechanism for generating target-specific partial observations (what a particular agent can perceive); and (3) a simulation procedure for how candidate actions update both physical and mental states. They instantiate this in MENTIS, a training-free, fully inspectable baseline system. MENTIS decomposes processing into several stages: state parsing from multimodal stories, generating what each target agent observes, decomposing actions, updating the coupled physical and mental states through transitions, and evaluating the value of each candidate action at the branch level. They test MENTIS and 8 modern LLM-based world models on a curated dataset of situated decision-making scenarios spanning text, images, and sounding-video stories.
AI.result: Experiments on a manually constructed and quality-controlled dataset of multimodal decision scenarios show that incorporating explicit mental state modeling significantly improves the prediction of human decisions compared to models that focus only on physical states. Across 8 modern LLM-based world models, those using the MWM-style explicit mental modeling better capture which actions humans actually choose. Further, the analyses uncover specific bottlenecks and limitations in current approaches to mental world modeling, suggesting where existing LLM-based models fall short in representing or updating mental states.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that explicit mental state modeling is essential for accurate prediction of human decisions and should be treated as a core part of world modeling rather than an auxiliary explanation layer. Mental World Modeling (MWM) is proposed as the next evolutionary step for world models: shifting from merely simulating physical environments to also simulating the minds of agents within them. The MENTIS instantiation provides a transparent baseline and reveals current limitations, guiding future research on building richer, more cognitively grounded world models that integrate physical and mental dynamics across modalities.
